review_title: SO Many Uses For Both Oils! I LOVE Them!
review_text:
I am finding SO many uses for Shiny Leaf's coconut and sweet almond oil! I do have some experience with coconut oil but this is my first time using sweet almond oil. Thanks the labels on the bottles, reviews and internet searches, I'm finding SO many ways to use these oils...sometimes together, sometimes individually.

Because I have terribly dry, sensitive skin, my main goal was to see how one or both oils could help protect my skin, especially now that winter has arrived and my skin is REALLY taking a beating. Both oils work well to hydrate and moisturize, so I mixed a few ounces of each in a mist bottle. After I bathe, I mist a combo of the oils over my skin to help hydrate and moisturize. The oils absorb quickly and do not leave an oily/greasy look OR feel to my skin. I'm already seeing a decrease in my dry skin/itchy red patches of skin. I experience NO discomfort whatsoever when misting these oils onto my sensitive skin. Both oils also work wonders on hair by moisturizing, hydrating, improving hair texture/strength, stimulate hair growth /thicken hair, and nourish the scalp to prevent dry, itchy flakes. In addition to using my combo of oils after bathing, I also give my hair a spray or two with the mister and sure enough, I'm seeing less hair in the drain and on my hairbrush after brushing. My hair is soft, smooth and shiny WITHOUT looking or feeling oily/greasy from the oil combo.

I use the coconut oil (alone) to help remove makeup, under and around my eyes to soften and reduce fine lines, I rub a small amount into my scalp (as does my husband) to help stimulate hair growth, on the kid's faces after their baths to soften (especially in cold weather!), on my nail beds every couple of days and a light amount on any patches of eczema/red skin. (It relieves the itching/burning and redness from eczema quickly!)

I use the sweet almond oil (alone) on dark circles under my eyes, a SMALL amount on split ends in my hair, a drop on chapped lips, I'm just starting to tinker with it for aromatherapy purposes. I recently learned that it can help fade scars so I've begun to rub some sweet almond oil into a scar on my finger to see what happens. If it helps, I'll then move on to a small facial scar I have. I'm also trying something on my own; just started doing this a few days ago. I get nosebleeds every single day, at least once a day, throughout the winter when the heat is on in the house. This started when I was 2 years old, I'm now 49 so I've experienced this my entire life. I now rub a small amount of sweet almond oil under my nostrils before bed. Since starting this, I continue to have nosebleeds. Yesterday, I had only one and it involved just a few drops of blood. I didn't whip through numerous tissues like normal. ONE tissue took care of it. (that's huge for me!) I have NO clue if its just a coincidence or if the sweet almond oil is helping in any way but I'm going to continue using it.

These oils are phenomenal! Both bottles are 16oz. I love the fact that they have normal caps on them but pumps for each bottle are included as well. The liquid of each is thinner oil than I expected, which I prefer. Both absorb quickly. Neither has a scent. I've found SO many uses for these oils, I can't wait to discover more. ( I'm SO happy with these oils, I recently purchased Shiny Leaf's biotin hair conditioner and cannot wait to try it! ) I find the price to be incredibly reasonable, especially since you're getting TWO bottles of oils! HIGHLY recommended!

*FYI...the mist bottle on the end in my photo is NOT included! I used one of my own mist bottles to combine both oils. You will get both bottles AND pumps that you see in my photo, NOT the mist sprayer!
100% happy thank you :-)

review_title: These are not USDA certified oils. 2 stars ✨
review_text:
First, I will say these oils seem fine. They work well together or apart, mixed into other skincare products or alone. I use these types of oils to make my own facial oil mix or to add to my moisturizer.
The thing I absolutely hate that companies do to try to sell their products is to say things that aren't true. The USDA does not certify oils - food, cosmetic, or otherwise. The fact that the bottle says this product is USDA certified on one side, and the other side says not intended for ingestion should speak volumes. The USDA certifies and regulates the welfare and production of food products; meaning products that you ingest. So, why on earth would they certify a product you cannot ingest? The bottle also makes outright claims of known cures from using these oils. There is no disclaimer on either bottle that states that these claims have not been approved or proven by the FDA, or whatever the disclaimer is that is mandatory. There are ingredients listed, one ingredient for each product, the oil, and that's it. Nothing tells how these oils were extracted. Therefore, we do not know if they are refined or unrefined. They probably don't know either. So you see, therein lies the lies and deception.
These oils would be much better if they weren't tied to lies. Because you know what they say about lies... if you tell one you have to tell more to keep up with the first one. Is what they say in the bottle really what's in the bottle? Are they pure oils or mixed with a lesser oil? Oils are greasy. If they are unrefined, why aren't they greasy? When you refine oils, you take away a lot of their natural properties and their nutritive value, is that why they aren't greasy? Because of the lies and lack of important information, I really don't know for sure what these oils are.
Because of the deceptive practices and claims made, I would not recommend these or any of their other oils.

This kit is a great deal!  I've been a devoted user of Korean skin care products.  For a while, I have preferred, out of several brands and types of sheet mask, the Benton Bee and Snail sheet mask.  Fantastic product!!!!  Firms, smooths, soothes.  It's great.  However, that's not why I purchased this set.  I have combo skin that leans towards oily in the heat.  Super oily T-zone.  After doing a ton of research, I decided to give the Benton Aloe Gel moisturizer a try.  I'd also heard great things about this foam cleanser.  I'm really enjoying the cleanser so far.  I wet my hands and face, use only a pea sized amount, rub my hands together to create the foam (not a soapy lather, but a thick and creamy foam), and work over my face.  I do this after oil cleansing.  This does a great job of picking up any oil residue and dirt, while leaving my face soft and refreshed.  Never tight and dry, which is the sign of an awful cleanser.  The gel moisturizer is okay.  Just okay.  I don't get as oily as I did with lotion moisturizers, which is great.  However, I don't have that supple, smooth feel that I'm used to and prefer.  I've actually noticed flaking around my nose, which is something I never dealt with after moisturizing.  A pea sized amount covers my entire face, it leaves a slightly tacky finish until absorbed ( I always let each of my products absorb for around 90 seconds before applying the next step), and is completely colorless.  Will I repurchase?  No, but I do suggest that you give this a try if your research and needs point you this direction.  Everyone's skin care needs can vary on several levels.  There are universal musts for good skin health, like cleansing daily, moisturizing, and using a good sunscreen.  There a a ton a variations of those products, though.  Finding the right routine and products can be a trial and error process.  The main thing is to stick to it.  The results are worth it!

I understand that there are differing opinions on this trimmer, but after using it back to back with the Remington Precision Pro MB-400 Titanium Vaccuum Mustache and Beard Trimmer, there is no comparison on the following counts:

1) quality of the trimming accessories - the Norelco has a flimsy cutting guide, and its all on the verge of breaking everytime you use it. Anyone who has had a previous Norelco product points this out.

2) a ridiculously designed sideburn trimmer - It is so hard to get the trimmer set-up! a poor design

The items above are enough to walk away from this device. The reviews that critique the vaccuum are probably being unrealistic. It is in part Norelco's fault - they set you up to expect more from the vaccuum than you get. But simple physics will tell you it is going to miss a lot of hair.

The Remington is superior in every way.

At the start I am giving it 3 stars because the bundles seem a little thin towards the ends. The ends are tangling and knotting as I finger through the hair. Not sure if something about shampoo and conditioner is going to bring them back to life but I plan to wash and reinstall it in a few days. It did well with blow drying and flat ironing it. A slight wave comes back to the hair over time. It held a decent curl. I curled it with my flat iron and set it with rods for about an hour. Attaching additional photos. I’d definitely buy the hair again. Still minimal shedding and minimal tangling. A quick brush through with my detangling brush and it’s back to life. This is my first time using bundles on myself and I can truly say I’m not disappointed. If it washes and reinstalls well even if the curls don’t come back I’m gonna bump it’s up to 5 stars. Where do I begin with this one... The ponytail arrived in good condition but with a strong smell to it. I needed to dye it dark brown before wearing so I stored it in the bag it came in for a month or two. When I took it out I noticed it was quite (really) tangled, but I was able to wash it and detangle it just fine, and it was shiny and bouncy after the first wash. After this is when things went downhill. I lifted the color so it could take the brown dye, but to my horror it was badly tangled again almost instantly. I went ahead and put the brown dye on so that I could do all of the serious detangling when it was done. However, it wasn't quite that simple.

I have pretty thick, long, curly, color treated hair myself but never have I had such a hard time detangling hair. I had soaked it overnight in conditioner, and when that didn't work, used almost an entire bottle of detangler but it didnt seem to do much, I couldn't pass a wide tooth comb through it at all. After HOURS of brushing it out from tip to roots, soaked in conditioner and detangler it finally got to a manageable place, and I had a whole handful of hair that had been shed in the process. I have heard that some hair suppliers clean and treat low quality hair from multiple donors with harsh chemicals that dissolve the cuticle, then re-coat it with silicon before selling it so it looks smooth... I am certain that is what happened. The worst part is there is no way to really tell until you wash it a couple of times, at which point it can't be returned. How convenient. Seriously, these people should go to jail for fraud, and amazon should be investigated for selling items from any random vendor in unregulated countries. What if an adult gets a life threatening allergic reaction, or a child is poisoned because a toy has lead on it, for example. Who is responsible then? This is not okay and I will be looking into my options to get my money back, although I will never get back the lost time. DONT BUY HAIR ON AMAZON!

review_text:

Have I ever told you how much I love trying new beauty products? In July I was fortunate enough to be sent the Pure Mauve Line of Products Made in Canada by Carapex Inc. of Chambly, Quebec to test out for 30 days and give my opinion. One of the reasons they thought I could benefit from this specific range is because I have written previously about the scalp psoriasis I’ve had for the past 18 months. The Tea Tree Oil is thought to help clear up the plaque that grows quickly over the scalp and sometimes other areas. This plaque appears very dry and can flake, crack, and if scratched can bleed and be very sore. Here’s a quote from the Carapex website about the Pure Mauve line “Due to our passion in the benefits of Tea Tree Oil, we developed this line of clean, natural, invigorating products. Only the purest, highest quality of Australian Tea Tree Oil has been utilized to work wonders on skin inflammation, breakouts and other conditions.”

So I don’t have to type it out every time, each Pure Mauve product I was sent has the name “Invigorating” and “with Tea Tree Oil”. I like the dark purple bottles because they’re different from anything else I have in the bathroom so stand out. I wear contacts so can barely see without them or my glasses and each bottle cap (except the Body Lotion) has a large silver letter on it so you know what it is you’re grabbing for. “S” for Shampoo, “C” for Conditioner, “T” for Toner, “M” for Moisturizer and “C” again for Cleanser. The Hair products are double the size of the facial ones, so you wouldn’t ever mix up the two “C”s.

I’ve been using everything exclusively for 30 days now and have 2/3 left still of the Lotion, Shampoo and Conditioner and 1/2 of the facial toner, cleanser, and moisturizer. I estimate the face items would last 2 months, the hair products for 3, and the body lotion would depend on whether you use it all over or just in certain areas. If you do not enjoy the smell of Tea Tree Oil, then these products are NOT for you. I joke that I smell like a health food store when I’m done my routine! Luckily the smell doesn’t last all day and you can still wear body mists or perfumes without the fragrance changing.

Final Results: To BEE (this gets a positive BUZZ)

As most Xenosaga fans are aware, Mr. Mitsuda created the soundtrack for Episode I, using the great Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. And that soundtrack received a lot of well-deserved praise and recognition. When it was announced that Ms. Kajiura would compose the music for Episode II, some of the fans where doubtful. During the short wait for Episode III, there were endless discussions on the many forums dedicated to Xenosaga as to who the fans would like to compose the music for the third episode. UPDATE: June 2018.....OK 5 years ago someone told me that it would grow on you. It has. Is still like the Te Deum better but what is really cool about this recording is it still has the original quadraphonic encoding. I am a lucky fellow to own an Involve Audio matrix decoder. This Australian company out of the blue developed a decoder for both SQ and QS matrix decoding with TODAYS technology. What this thing does for this recording will blow your mind!!!!! It is like you are sitting in the cathedral with the ambiance totally engulfing you with no smear or detriment to the excellent stereo separation up front... Stunning. By the way dear reader, the Involve Audio device is fantastic on MOST of my lp's and cd's along with anything recorded in stereo. If the recording was made in a concert hall it is amazing at extracting the acoustics and putting them in the rear channels. With most of my 80's and 90's rock it is also fantastic...like recordings from ELO and Alan Parsons etc... Classical recordings can just astound you regardless of date as long as recording is stereophonic. And of course, if you own Quad records the result is like discreet channels. review_title: This review is for the paperback edition
review_text:
Joe Quail was climbing a dream stairway. Below him, magical towers poked through a fading sunset. Above him, the stairs soared and swooped dizzily until they reached the stars.

The Princess of Afterdark was calling him. 'Where are you, Joe?'

'I'm coming,' he said sleepily.

At last Joe found her, on the highest step of all, her wild hair blowing in the night sky. 'Who do you need me to fight this time? Trolls, dragons, evil enchanters?'

'No, Joe, it's your world which is in trouble now. And the danger is much closer than you think--'

But before she could explain, the air filled with horrible sighs. The stairway slowly cracked down the middle. As the half of the stair with the princess on it began to drift away, she cried, 'Wake up, Joe! Wake up, before it's too late!'

Vasco Shine is a threat to every child because he steals their dreams. In the second book of the Afterdark series Joe, Kevin and pale, prickly Flora have to go to the fantastic Kingdom of Afterdark, where nothing and no one is what it seems, to stop him. The three friends travel through paradise islands, magical dream fields and terrifying dangers searching for the Pearl of the Deep, the key to Vasco's wickedness ...

It isn't necessary to have read the first Afterdark book to enjoy this enchanting and imaginative novel. Annie Dalton, writing with her usual grace and flair, manages to pack an amazing amount of action and characterisation into 183 pages and (as can be seen from the above quote, which is the beginning of the book) she plunges the reader straight into the magic and excitement of Afterdark with the story's first sentence.

review_title: The Best Recording of Sibelius' Violin Concerto - Bar None
review_text:
Sibelius' Violin Concerto by Dylana Jenson and Eugene Ormandy definitely holds a place in my list of "ten records I'd take with me to a desert isle."

Among violin concertos, the Sibelius is obligatory for any soloist who wishes to be taken seriously, but I do not believe this piece has been sufficiently recognised for its place in the Sibelius repertoire. In Harold Johnson's 1959 biography, "Jean Sibelius," the author is at a loss when it comes classifying this among Sibelius' other masterworks. This may in part be due to the treatment the Concerto had previously been given by violinists - as a virtuoso piece, rather than a composition written in Sibelius' own inimitable style. This is understandable, given that Sibelius was an accomplished solo violinist.

Prior to obtaining this recording, the only two I owned were by Heifetz (with Hendl/Chicago Symphony) and Perlman (Leinsdorf/Boston Symphony). While I admire Heifetz' sterling performance, it seems aloof from the actual music itself, brilliantly and expertly played, but lacking in depth. The Perlman just never did anything for me.

This CD by Dylana Jenson with Eugene Ormandy and the Philadelphia Orchestra was her debut recording, which RCA chose to showcase in its then-new digital series. What makes it so satisfying is that it is by far the most Sibelian performance I've heard, then or since (and I own 11 different recordings). This is more difficult than it sounds. I have found most violinists to have rather "inbred" perspectives in regards to the repertoire for the solo violin - they tend to "interpret" a piece of music from the standpoint of the music out there for their instrument (which is logical), rather than understanding the composition's place within the composer's output. Hence, a brilliant performer such as Heifetz sounds as though he doesn't "get it," despite his sound musicianship. This approach by lesser virtuosos, such as Sarah Chang in her 1996 performance with the Berliner Philharmoniker and Mariss Jansons (himself a dedicated Sibelian), falls flat on its face.

But the Jenson recording does not "come close"; it's *there.* Jenson, who recorded this when she was twenty, obviously holds an affection for the music of Sibelius and beautifully gets under the skin of the piece. Her playing is seemingly paradoxical: Her timing is so mathematically precise that one could set a metronome to it and her execution is so matter-of-fact, that it sounds inevitable. And yet, this could never for a minute be mistaken for indifference, for her performance comes across as inspired and impassioned. Through her performance, you can hear that the Sibelius Concerto belongs not in a category by itself (as Johnson suggests) but thematically with the First Symphony and "En Saga" and structurally with the Second and Fifth Symphonies.

From the opening of the first movement (Allegro moderato), Jenson's violin subtly rises from within the ostinato of the upper strings played in pp-p, placing her violin firmly at the helm, but never outside, of the orchestra. Eugene Ormandy's conducting goes a long way towards the seamless integration between soloist and orchestra - as with so many other soloists, Ormandy places the Philadelphia in the service of providing a sympathetic accompaniment. The genius of Ormandy (and Jenson) is that the orchestra is never in a subordinate role. Throughout the opening movement there are intimate passages in which Jenson's solo violin beautifully communicates with orchestra soloists, such as the cellist, the bassoonist and clarinetist. There is one passage in which Jenson's violin and the solo 'cello repeatedly exchange a handful of notes between each other in so simple and understated a manner, that it conjures in the mind's eye two lovers meeting, then parting, in the night.

Dylana Jenson's violin (a treasured Guarnerius del Gesu) has such a warm tone that it almost sounds like a viola and her bowing is smooth without ever having to over-rely upon vibrato. Her playing clearly achieves the Sibelian ideal in sound: Her instrument sounds as though it is playing from within the orchestra, though she never becomes subsumed in the ensemble.

Nowhere is this more evident than in the second movement, Adagio di molto. I've heard many a performance in which the soloist tries to "impart meaning" to this movement by letting the bow linger just a shade too long on the strings, which only ruins the whole effect intended by the composer. From listening to Jenson's simple and persuasive interpretation, it is refreshing to hear this movement interpreted gently, honestly and forcefully, the meaning found where it had been all along - in the notes as written by the composer.

The Finale (Allegro ma non tanto) is where Jenson really gets to show her "chops." This movement runs the whole gamut of difficulty in bowing and fingering, and Jenson brings the same expertness she does in the earlier movements in building towards the finale's climax tautly and suspensefully, yet without tearing the concerto away from its thematic roots. A couple of the runs sound so breathtakingly impossible (without sounding in the least incongruous to the thematic material) that you realise that you're listening to perhaps to the most difficult of concertos; difficult not only technically, but one that demands an implicit understanding on the part of the soloist, conductor and orchestra. This recording more than delivers on all three accounts.

Saint-Saens' "Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso" is likewise imparted with the same maturity on Jenson's part as the Sibelius: As music, first and foremost. Yet, unlike the Sibelius, Jenson realises she's got a "showpiece" on her hands, and plays accordingly. Yet, as Toscanini would even conduct Rossini's "William Tell" Overture with the same thoughtfulness and passion that he would "Turandot," Jenson never comes across as hackneyed, but rather musically committed to this piece. There is a section in which her playing deftly shifts gears into a wistful, reflective interlude, then effortlessly builds to the quicksilver finale without missing a beat.

Altogether, a brilliant recording by one of the great violinists of our time.

review_title: A Truly Classic Christmas Album, A MUST HAVE!
review_text:
This has been my favorite Christmas album since I bought it at a Hallmark store in 1995. Who knew? It is a classic as much as the Bing Crosby and the Charlie Brown Christmas albums are. The real tragedy is that it is a rare and obscure title. You can't really blame people because they don't know that Glen Close can not only hold her own with a world renown opera singer, but has a voice that is truly amazing, clear and bright over an orchestra and chorus. Why hasn't she produced other albums? The orchestra, chorus and recording are superb, every song is wonderful with "Ding Dong Merrily on High" an incredible finish. It's a crime they didn't make a DVD out of the performance.

If I ever meet Glen Close I won't gush over her outstanding acting, it will be for producing a classic, and my favorite, Christmas album which I listen to, over and over, every December. If you like full throated, joyous classic Christmas music, you must have this album.

Sir Colin Davis is known for his Berlioz recordings by fans and critics alike. This, to my knowledge, is Davis' only recording Berlioz's "Requiem" and what a fine one it is!

I have three other versions of this requiem: Munch's on RCA, Spano's and Shaw's both on Telarc. I have heard all four versions I own and have done some comparisons. One thing remarkably clear in Davis' recording is his incredible ear for the innerworkings of the structure and how to bring out the darker elements of the composition. The choral singing is outstanding quite possibly some of the best I've heard on any recording. The orchestral accompaniment is also evenly paced, well-balanced, and powerful when it needs to be. The London Symphony Orchestra also plays great.

Another bonus for me is Philips warm analog sound. I own many (and I do mean many) Philips recordings and they always have such great warmth and clarity. This recording is no different.

The performance of "Symphony Funebre et Triomphale" is also very good and I have actually already heard this performance in this set: [[ASIN:B0000041MZ Berlioz: Complete Orchestral Works]], which is now sadly out-of-print.

This is the greatest recording I've heard of the very difficult to play and sing "Requiem." I'm still on the lookout for a more superior recording, but I have yet to find one. Highly recommended.

The Rubinstein Piano Concerto #3 is classic romantic fare. What lacks in creativity or emotional depth, is made up by virtuoso showcasing in the outer movements, as is to be expected, particularly in the closing Allegro.
Kabalevsky #3 is a very logical coupling. More complex and emotionally involving than Rubinstein's #3, it is nonetheless a reactionary work. Composed in 1952, at the time when Ligeti was writing his Musica Ricercata, sounds like something Tchaikovsky may have written a century earlier.
I have no comparison recordings, but Robert Preston seems to have no problems meeting Rubinstein technical requirements, and Kabalevski interpretational ones. Freeman and the Westphalians are good accompanists. The remarkably natural sound is the best thing of this recording: closing my eyes it feels like seating in the 10th row of a good concert hall, right in front of the piano.

"Foothills" is an immediately accessible work of about 14 minutes by the American composer Scott Pender (b. 1959). Pender studied composition as a graduate and undergraduate at Peabody Conservatory before receiving a Fullbright grant to study with English composer Gavin Bryars. He has composed in a variety of genres and his music has been performed to critical acclaim in the United States and Europe. Pender has lived in Washington, D.C for 35 years, and "Foothills" is performed by the Takoma Ensemble, a chamber orchestra located in Takoma Park under the direction of Victoria Gau. Pender and I have become friends through activity in a classical music club in Washington, D.C., and I was pleased that he offered me the opportunity to review this new work which was recorded at the Peabody Institute in February, 2014.

"Foothills" takes a lovingly nostalgic look at rural America in both its music and its background. The work was commissioned by the North Georgia Chamber Symphony which premiered the work in 2013 in Dahlonega, Georgia, under conductor Laurin Smith. The work will be featured as the soundtrack to an upcoming documentary "Pieced Together", scheduled for release in early 2015. The film describes the development of quilt squaring trails which can be found rural areas in 40 states.

Scored for small string orchestra and piano, the work is in four short movements with strong suggestions of American folk music. The work is lyrical, rhythmical and dancelike. The orchestra predominates in the early part of the work but the balance between orchestra and piano shifts gradually so that the solo piano, performed by David Iskowitz, has the lead role in the final movement.

The work opens with a fast vigorous movement in which plucked strings contrast with a lyrical theme. The second movement, "languorous, not hurried" has a flowing theme in the strings over a quiet rippling piano, which has a larger role than in the opening movement. The third movement, "slow, lyrical" has a melancholy cast in which strings and piano are evenly balanced in a duet. The final movement, "Lively, Swinging" is joyful and triumphal in character. After a brief, angular introduction from the orchestra, the piano is featured in the conclusion over a string background. I found "Foothills" simple, emotive, and endearing.

This is a short CD consisting only of the 14-minute "Foothills" and is probably intended to introduce Pender and his new composition to a broader audience. I hope it succeeds in its aim. I enjoyed getting to know "Foothills" and Scott Pender's music in this brief CD.

review_title: Good Quality Recording of An Interesting Elvis Concert.
review_text:
"If You Talk in Your Sleep" is a recording taken from Elvis's August 19, 1974 show in Vegas. His first show of the season, it's held in historical regard by fans for its unique set list and committed performance; in attempt to change things up, Elvis dropped several songs he had been performing regularly for the last two or three years (including his standard opener "See See Rider") and instead put some new and rare songs in the set list.

The rarely performed numbers are performed strongly; "Down in the Alley," a bluesy leftover from the "Spinout" sessions, is given a strong workout and is a nice treat for die-hards, while the eerily self-reflective "Good Time Charlie's Got the Blues" probably hit close to home for The King at the time and is given a sincere, passionate rendition. He's in strong voice for the time period, and gives belters like "Never Been to Spain" and "Bridge Over Troubled Water" the muscle they need. New singles like "If You Talk in Your Sleep" and his hit cover of Chuck Berry's "Promised Land" are received warmly and performed well.

As was typical by this time, classics like "Hound Dog," "Love Me Tender," and "Can't Help Falling in Love" are tossed up with little to no investment. Also, the dry soundboard tape leaves much to be desired. Still, this is a pretty unique show in Elvis's career and one worth seeking out.

review_title: Berlioz: Romantic AND Classicist-with French polish
review_text:
Some people may think that the conductor Colin Davis is boring, but I find his approach to Berlioz quite appropriate. Although some conductors (like, say, Leonard Bernstein) may want to really give Berlioz "the works" as the strive to play up the composers wildly imaginative music; what should also be preserved is Berlioz' more sophisticated and delicate side. Berlioz is easy to overplay. Davis' method of understatement does the music justice in that it allows the simple and organic beauty of the Requiem to be heard. Yes, Berlioz was a powerful Romantic, but also something of a classicist with some French polish.

The Requiem itself is a wonderful piece of music, as whatever recording you obtain of it will probably reveal. It is, first of all a very, very, long work that keeps the listener interested through profound solemness, as well as, thoughtful creativity. The second to last movement with tenor solo is quite moving. As the soloist sings "santos", the crashing cymbals gently accentuate. The final movement is also quite mesmerizing as the orchestra lovingly modulates and creates a trance-like atmosphere. It is indeed a moving experience-and I am not much a fan of most requiems!

In the early days of the CD era, many companies, large and small, produced CD's of existing LP or cassette products to exploit the market for the new medium. This series of "Super Oldies of the 60's" was one of those; however the CD's did not always exactly mirror the LP's.

This volume, number two in the series, gathers together 16 top-40 early 60's hits with most, save two, having made the top-20. Although these were all major hits in their day, some of the tunes included here are seldom found on CD reissues and therein lies the appeal. Alongside Del Shannon's commonplace "Hats Off to Larry" and the Chiffons' ubiquitous "He's So Fine", are found "Midnight Special from Paul Evans (of "Seven Little Girls" fame), and the G-Clefs' "I Understand".

Technically, all the CD's in this series reflect the early days of CD reissues. These tracks were mostly, if not all, taken from vinyl and reveal some surface noise on some tracks. On the positive side, they do not seem to have been subjected to attempts at "cleaning up" and therefore do not exhibit the overly compressed sound found on some CD's in the market. Having been taken from masters destined for vinyl pressings (with the high end pumped up to compensate for the high-end loss when going to vinyl), some of the tracks exhibit more volume at the upper end.

In this particular volume, all the tracks are mono or electronically rechanneled with the exception of track 12. While not technically in the class of Ace, Bear or Rhino reissues, the CD's in this series do offer fans of the genre a few hard-go-find tracks (that are becoming harder to find) in the waning days of the music CD format.

Perhaps the erratic releases, label-switching and stylistic turnabouts made his catalog more of a challenge to reissue. So when a career-spanning, multi-label compilation CD comes along, it is something of an event.

In this collection from the somewhat mysterious and hard-to-trace Black Tulip label are gathered together all of Carlton's top-100 pop-charting tunes from his first, "Competition Ain't Nothin' " in the late `60's (as by Little Carl Carlton), to his final appearance on the pop charts in 1981 with "She's a Bad Mama Jama". His biggest hit by far, the song that took him furthest into mainstream pop stylistically and in many ways became his signature song, "Everlasting Love", leads off this set. The remaining tunes included are his other charting and non-charting singles and a selection of album cuts. All told, though hardly a complete telling, the generous 25 tracks here represent a decent anthology of Carlton's recorded works.

While understandably not of original master quality and while discernable variation exists, sound quality here is surprising good overall. Most of the tracks (1,5-6,8,11-21) are stereo with the remainder in mono. The insert provides no more than the track listing so as with other labels of this type, the recordings themselves are the only find here.

Given the relative dearth of CD's available for Carlton's musical output, this decent collection of his music fills a long-standing void in the music collector's library.

review_title: Grand, Expansive, Probing Performance of Beethoven's Great Seventh Symphony
review_text:
Having just finished listening to Herbert Kegel's recording, with the Dresden Philharmonic, of Beethoven's Seventh Symphony, I was somewhat startled to realise that the Dresdner Philharmonie (know in English as the "Dresden Philharmonic Orchestra") turns out to be such an exceptionally fine orchestra! I would not have expected Dresden to have another such excellent orchestra in addition to the famous Sächsische Staatskapelle Dresden (known in English simply and usually as the "Dresden Staatskapelle Orchestra") but, yes, Dresden is a city of considerable orchestral excellence, indeed. The Philharmonic of that city may not be quite on the supreme level of the Staatskappelle, one of the world's greatest orchestras of all, but it comes pretty darn close!

Of course, the Germans are so cultivated and they support the arts so magnificently, that it is not surprising that some German cities have more than one top-line orchestra. All that one has to do, by way of further example, is to think of Munich, with its civic and also radio symphony orchestras, both of them among the finest internationally. Leipzig, for its part, where Kegel formerly had directed the second-stringer Mitteldeutscher Rundfunks Sinfonieorchester (Leipzig Radio Orchestra) which does not come up to the level of the city's own Gewandhaus Orchestra of of the orchestras in Munich and Dresden, either, in that regard, The Gewandhausorchester (in English terms, the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra) is superior by a considerable margin to the Leipzig orchestra that Kegel conducted in that recording of Brahms' Second Symphony. Indeed, the Staatskapelle and Gewandhaus orchestras both are of the very top rank of orchestras internationally. However, in Dresden, the Philharmonic holds its own quite well, "thank-you-very-much".

The Dresden Philharmonic's, double bass section is really something to savour; that instrument having been the one on which I attained greatest proficiency, anyway, it should not be surprising that I tend to listen from the bottom upwards so much of the time, and what I hear in this recording is very pleasing in that regard. The basses do not have the incisive edge and attack that make the "old" (pre-Ozawa) Boston Symphony (especially under Koussevitzky and Leinsdorf) and New York Philharmonic (under Bernstein) orchestras so supremely exciting, but the Dresden dudes, indeed, fare quite well as bass players and as together as a section, in my estimation. The entire orchestra holds up well to such close aural scrutiny.

Kegel's approach to Beethoven's Seventh Symphony in Dresden is at the antipodes of Leinsdorf;s supreme recorded performance in Boston, Kegel's being a memorably fine performance on its own very different terms. Leinsdorf's Boston S.O. recording is electrifyingly kinetic, thrillingly the stuff of "life or death" struggle and energy. In that regard. Except in being so much better, Leinsdorf's own effort is along the lines of Toscanini's 1930s recordings of the symphony, but, thankfully, less "tightassed" and obsessive than Toscanini had been. Leinsdorf makes greater space for the Romantic elements in the work than Toscanini had done so. Toscanini is more strictly and invariably classical in expression, very powerfully so, in a somewhat rigidly unbending sort of way. Kegel, on the other hand, is more expansive in pacing and concept than either Leinsdorf or Torscanini, but Kegel does not sound at all indifferent to the genuine style and content of Beethoven's epoch-straddling music. The tempi which Kegel sets are slower than Toscnini's or Leinsdorf's. I did not measure them or make direct A-B comparisons with a metronome, but Kegel's tempi do feel, at least, to be less propulsive.

I would characterise Kegel's performance as quite measured, carefully calibrated (especially in moving from one movement to the next to emphasise contrasts between them), and, well, wise and deliberate (not the latter word in the sense of slow, but rather in that of setting forth its own interpretively particular stance). Kegel's phrasing is, unusually, more lyrical, sustained, and legato than one normally hears, although not at all weakly flabby and even a bit crude in that regard, as in Monteux' doddering manner, as with the London Symphony Orchestra, at that maestro's worst (in repertory for which Monteux in old age does not excel so memorably as he did lifelong in Russian and French music); in his prime Monteux had conducted Beethoven's symphonies and overtures superbly, but the ageing maestro did so much less reliably well in the last decade or so of his life. Anyway, Kegel's recording has a strong interpretive profile of its own, one that, in its own way, is a welcome contrast to Leinsdorf's taughtly sublime recording. As one may notice in my reviews, I tend to prefer (although not invariably) forward-pressing, high energy performances, so long, of course, as they do not become merely frenetic or superficially showy.

There are some keenly subtle transitions that Kegel makes, if one listen attentively, not only within the symphony's movements but also between them. Kegel does not conduct the Seventh as though it were entirely of one fabric alone. For one thing, to take a clue from orchestral balances, at first he seems to under-emphasise the tympani, especially in comparison to Leinsdorf, who makes quite a feast (a welcome one) of them. However, as one movement follows another, the percussion becomes incrementally more prominent. By the last movement, the kettledrums are searing in their impact. That is a very interesting and subtle way to handle percussion. In general, Kegel seems to tighten the expressive screws noticeably from one movement to the following one as the work proceeds along its course. This has the effect of offering quite a lot of variety within the work.

All of this is far from saying that I do not continue to prefer Leinsdorf's taut approach throughout that conductor's own performance of the work, but merely that Kegel's way with Beethoven's Seventh Symphony rewards the listener amply in its own manner. I shall be coming back rather often to Kegel's recording of the Seventh, since I revel in alternative approaches, if they be valid ones, even if I have strong preferences for what I like best among recorded performances of such great music as Beethoven's mighty Seventh Symphony most assuredly is.

Kegel's Dresden recording of Beethoven's Second Symphony makes for a genial disc companion to the Seventh on this CD. The orchestra's excellent playing and ensemble work make the conductor's approach, emphasising grace and mellifluous lyricism above the work's potential for humour and energetic drive. This is not to say that Kegel ignores such aspects of the score, but rather that his approach is solidly grounded, large in gesture, lyrical, and often more dance-like, when Beethoven's rhythms encourage that, making a sun-filled, mellow feast of this delightful music.

Compared to so many other rival recorded performances of the Second, which number among them the great accounts of Sir Thomas Beecham (with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra) and of Leonard Bernstein (the recording which he made with the New York Philharmonic Orchestra being the one in mind), Kegel's recording holds its own. However, I have to admit that I do prefer the sense of adventure, thrusting energy, and of jovial humour that Bernstein brings to the fore in his great rendition rather more than Kegel opts for as an alternative to emphasising also such characteristics of this symphony. For those who prefer a more gentle and reflective approach, rather than the likes of Bernstein's, to Beethoven's Second Symphony, Kegel's excellent work with the Dresden Philharmonic, well recorded, make it a wise choice, especially since the Seventh Symphony on the same disc is so good and very much in the same interpretive mode.

review_title: FORGET THE INSTRUMENTS--IT'S A GREAT PERFORMANCE
review_text:
A sticker on the cover of this set proudly proclaims “First time on period instruments.” Fortunately that is not the only attraction on this recording. To be honest, I don’t hear anything really different in the sound of these “period instruments.” There is no moment while listing to this recording where I found myself thinking, “Wow, I never really heard the music articulated that way before.” I think the further along the spectrum of music history you advance, the more diminished are the returns on using “authentic” instruments. I suppose eventually we will have a recording of Gershwin’s “Rhapsody in Blue” performed only on instruments built before 1924—which some purists will no doubt hail as a “revelation.”

Forget the instruments; what is most salient about this recording is that it’s simply a great performance. The chorus and orchestra are first-rate, bringing out every detail without making a fetish of it, phrasing beautifully while wringing every bit of excitement out of the music that Verdi composed into it. For this I credit John Eliot Gardiner’s sensitive and insightful conducting, not the supposed authenticity of the instruments being used (I have heard Gardiner achieve the same level of musical artistry in live performances of other works with modern symphony orchestras), and the recorded presence is stunning—this Dies Irae will knock the grille-cloths off your speakers and can stand alongside the best of them. The quartet of solo voices is lovely, perhaps not with the powerhouse operatic star quality evident on some other recordings, but they seem to suit Gardiner’s conception. Rather than expressing dramatic fire, horror and dread in broad, Technicolor strokes, they seem to focus more inwardly on matters of mystical faith, a completely valid approach for such a work. I would never want to be without Solti’s recording, which features four of the greatest operatic voices of his time, but no one should hesitate to acquire this superb reading, whether you intend to supplement it with other versions or not. Although to be sure this is one of a handful of masterworks that deserve to be represented by more than recording in your home library. The Four Sacred Pieces included are also exquisitely sung and make a fine bonus, but the Mass performance would be worth buying even without it.

.... from von Karajan and the usual lumbering, rumbling warhorse symphonic performances of the Requiem. The essence of this performance is not the use of period instruments but rather of "period sensibilities" by an orchestra and chorus that fully cooperate with their conductor's interpretation. Only the reeds, trumpets and drums sound radically different from modern instruments in timbre, but the articulations and bowings of the strings sound quite a lot less mushy than those on other recordings. Gardiner takes several movements at tempi that will surprise listeners familiar with older, stuffier versions. Likewise he takes the opening 'requiem aeternam' at a passionate adagio, pianissimo, setting your ears up for the thunderous kyrie.

It's the orchestra and the chorus that carry this performance to the heights. I'm not so enthusiastic about the four soloists - soprano Luba Orgonasova, mezzo Anne Sofie von Otter, tenor Luca Canonici, and bass Alastair Miles. The two ladies do a certain amount of scooping and swooping, shaking and quaking, while the two gentlemen don't really have the most abundant voices. All four have frequent pitch problems; Verdi must be harder to sing in tune than the notes look on the page, since pitch problems plague many recordings of his operas as well. That's my reason for giving this CD only four stars. Nevertheless, the "whole" is great enough to carry along the "parts."

Numerous critics consider the Requiem to be the finest music that Verdi ever composed. I readily agree. If you have been disappointed in the music as such of some of the operas -- as I have been -- you may be astonished at the vigor of his composition in this huge Requiem.

Postscript: Listening at home, on my higher-end system, I have a slightly different impression. The two men singers have more 'character' in their voices than I heard before. The 'whole' is a bit of a chore to listen to; it sounds a little too episodic (Verdi's fault, not Gardiner's) and it's strenuous because of the extreme, explosive changes of volume. You have to play it loud enough to hear the detail in the quietest sections, but then your eardrums will be at risk in the very loud tutti sections. That's the nature of the beast.

This is a Philips Duo CD so it has been compiled from various LPs recorded in London and Amsterdam in 1968, 1969, 1971, 1981 and 1983. The soloists are Stephen Kovacevich (playing the piano pieces Opp. 116, 117, 118, 119, and the Variations and Fugue on a Theme of Handel); Dinorah Varsi (playing the two Rhapsodies and the Piano Pieces Op.76); and Adam Harasiewicz (playing the Variations on a Theme of Paganini). The two sets of Variations here - on themes by Handel and by Paganini - were composed in 1861/62 when Brahms was in his late 20s. But the remaining pieces were composed betwen1879 and 1893, just four years before his death. It is these pieces that give the title of the CD. The playing is fine, the piano tone quite warm and soft and not as brittle as it often sounds in more modern recordings. They are mostly analogue recordings (except Opp. 116 and 118 which are digital). I have lived happily with this double CD since it was released two decades ago and I would not want to be without it. The second of the four Intermezzi in Op.118 has gained a certain extra popularity recently as it is featured in some of the episodes of Robert Parker's Jesse Stone thrillers on TV.

These performances of four Schubert sonatas are taken from live concerts by Alfred Brendel in England, the Netherlands and Germany. All four display the pianist's typical technical control and interpretive thoughtfulness, with an added intensity from the presence of an audience (though there is little if any intrusive noise). Perhaps the prize of this two-CD set is the G major Sonata D. 894; the rapt intensity of its long Molto Moderato first movement, the lyricism of the Andante, and the charm of the Minuetto and final Rondo have never been conveyed better in a superbly balanced performance. The other three sonatas, while of course excellently played, are not quite on this level; the first movement of the great posthumous A major D. 959 is exciting but lacks the magisterial poise of Brendel's studio rendition, while the accelerated coda of the Rondo finale somehow fails to whip up the requisite excitement of the long journey concluded. Brendel's Scherzo of the posthumous B-flat sonata D. 960 (Schubert's final piano work) catches the "delicatezza" of the tempo mark perfectly, but the finale is slightly untidy. Most interesting for Brendel fans is his only recording of the earlier B major Sonata D. 575, which remains a slightly disjointed effort from the composer despite many incidental charms and ravishing playing from the pianist in the slow movement. Still, this is a collection that will repay many listenings, in common with all of Brendel's work.

review_title: WOW- Great album. WHY no digital version???
review_text:
This guys voice is a freaking GIFT. Seriously- what a great rock singer. I've always liked Jefferson Starship and Starship. However- I absolutely was NOT a fan of the 'Nothing's Gonna Stop Us Now' type of stuff. 'Rosemary Clooney songs' indeed (Grace Slick quote about that period). I never was a big fan of Grace Slick, she's ok but other than the Jefferson Airplane hits, just never got what she brought to this band. Never a fan of the Paul Kantner songs, usually just monotone singing with lyrics that didn't catch my attention. Not to be insulting there, it just wasn't my thing.

HOWEVER- Mickey Thomas. Completely different story. He was the reason I got into these guys at all. When I heard 'Find Your Way Back', I was INSTANTLY hooked. What a great song- an electric 12 string and THAT VOICE together? Holy Awesome. I never get tired of that song. The harder rocking JS/S stuff was what kept me interested. When they went softer, I, like so many others, lost the desire to listen to them because it was just so dull to me. It all sounded the same. The edges from "Find Your Way Back", "Jane", "Layin it on the Line" all got shaved off and the record company turned the band into something else. While I miss the days of buying albums, etc. I don't miss record company suits guiding bands into 'doing it for the money'.

After "Knee Deep In the Hoopla" got driven into the ground by what around that time started to become corporate radio (and also Mtv), I just got tired of hearing them. Their next album ("No Protection") absolutely lost me and they had clearly removed all their edges and had become completely uninteresting to me. Not even Thomas' pipes could rescue dull songs and even duller production. I bought "Love Among the Cannibals" because it was in a cutout bin, so many years ago. Quite honestly, I think I have only listened to one or two songs off it after I moved my collection to a media server and that's been within only the last month or so.

I lost track of Mickey over the years, but of course had heard about the incident with Starship's drummer- horrifying and I remember feeling bad for him for sure. I had forgotten about him until I heard 'Jane' recently somewhere. Hmm, wonder what that guy is up to these days?

Well, he's put together his own version of Starship and is still touring constantly. I checked out some of his live stuff on Youtube and the guy still absolutely HAS IT. ALL the range, all the runs. Wow. As a wannabe vocalist myself, it's inspirational to hear a rock guy at his age (sorry Mickey) that absolutely hasn't lost a note. In fact, he's gained an edge. Not 'gotten rough' as Journey's Steve Perry did around Frontiers (who continued to lose his range), but Mickey can still sing cleanly and now has gained some rock edge that he can turn on and off at will. AND- He still, as of 2019 sings those great songs in the same, original keys. Quite an achievement as these (and Journey's) are some of the toughest songs in the rock catalog.

This album features that, AND it brings together the missing edge that had vanished from latter Starship stuff. The album also has a bit of the easier-going vibe that the poppier version of the band had but it hasn't managed to have the edges shaved off of it. Produced by Foreigner bassist Jeff Pilson, he's done a great job of writing most of this and giving Mickey back the balls that made him so good in the first place.

For me, the best track on it (by a mile) is "Technicolor Black & White". It really kicks a**. It's got a Zeppelinish guitar riff, political lyrics, and Mickey's hard-edged voice. The song's lyrics are spot on and it's just a brilliant sounding track. This would've been a hit in 79 and really packs a punch. Bravo on this track! Huge chorus, even huger bridge (remember 'Bridges', kids??? oh, how I've missed them!). Dear Mr. Thomas- If you are looking for a 'direction' or a 'north star' to steer towards, this is absolutely IT. Whatta great tune. Keep in mind, I'm writing this just a few days after the 2020 election and this song, done in 2018, is completely relevant right now.

The rest of the songs are also very very good and Thomas' delivery on all of them is dead on.

The only song that really doesn't grab me that much is the last track, written by Diane Warren. While I didn't have a huge problem with Cheap Trick's "The Flame", you kind of know what you're going to get with her stuff and it just offers no surprises. At least to this point in my listening, this is the weakest track for me. It starts out great with a gospel choir sound, and I'm expecting that Mickey's going to go for it and give us some of his R&B chops... but it veers into "Nothing's Gonna Stop Us Now" territory, which isn't what I'm after with Mickey Thomas these days (Warren wrote both). review_title: Great score, glad to see it released
review_text:
The previous soundtrack release for the 1985 classic vampire film 'Fright Night' had featured only the songs from the film; completely absent was Brad (The Terminator) Fiedel's chilling score. This release by Intrada puts all that right.

In a similar way to 'The Terminator', which he had scored the year before, Brad Fiedel relies quite heavily on synthesizers and a 'technological' type of score to create a distinctly 'creepy' feeling which is apparent throughout the score, rather than relying on a strictly orchestral soundtrack. The creepy seduction theme 'Come to Me' is featured in at least 3 tracks; it first appears in 'Window Watching' where young Charley catches his next-door neighbor in the act of revealing his vampirism as he attacks a call-girl; the second time it appears, the seductive vampire Jerry Dandridge has kidnapped Charley's girlfriend Amy (Amanda Bearse, 'Married...with Children') and the famous seduction scene takes place as the fiendish Dandridge attacks Amy. The liner notes give a superb description of the tracks and the events in the film they correspond to.

Great score. Welcome to 'Fright Night'!

Bad news: the sound sucks. If that really bothers you, stop here.

Good news: this disc (and its companion) are good enough to be canon - altering. What the Hell were they putting in the water in Fort Worth, Texas back in the early '50's? These discs reveal Carter and Bradford as really major duo improvisors, and if they were better - distributed, would remove these two musicians from Ornette's shadow once and for all. Even though some of Carter's ensemble projects are conceptually remarkable, the fairly workmanlike rhythm section often drags them down to the "specialist" level. But this is improvised music for the ages. Bradford's middle register lyricism took a totally different path from Don Cherry's more Pollock - like blobs and blats, and Carter makes the best case I've heard for the clarinet in Free Jazz. Is this Free Jazz? For want of a better term...yes.
Carter is amazing, with his shrieks and his multiphonics. He makes a kind of bridge between the Ornette - y world of First Generation Free Jazz and the more sound - oriented work of the "Second Wave" - AACM and like that. But he is really unique, and any such attempt to place him within a stylistic continuum will run into pitfalls.Bradford has the whole history of Jazz Trumpet in his lines and his sound, and yet one is never aware of any studied eclecticism. But what is most wonderful on this disc is the way these two play TOGETHER. They give no quarter, maintaining their differences and the distinctions between their approaches to language. At the same time, they echo each other, with such a phenomenal shared ear for register and timbre. There is no grandstanding, no hyperbole, no attempt at Grand Statements which would demolish the carefully calibrated scale of these performances. And yet there is such a wide emotional and expressive range within each and every track. I will resist the desire to go track by track - you get the idea, I hope. I'll just close by fervently thanking the Emanem label for making this great music available.

Simple Minds’ umpteenth live album “Live In the City of Angels”, a four disc 40 song extravaganza, is so polished in its recording that at many points one can forget it’s live and mistake it for a studio album. And that’s the bottom line: if you like your live album complete with its quirks, audience participation and/or interference, and uneven and over exaggerated levels then Angels may leave you wanting. If, however, you like your recordings highly polished and sounding smooth with carefully controlled levels of production then Angels may shine bright in your ears and eyes. Me? I see the merits in both places but I like the clear and separate sounds produced herein. Also to my liking is that the Minds cover so much of their catalog which, I suppose, isn’t hard to do with 40 songs. All musicians shine, Burchill’s guitar comes through crisply and tightly, and Kerr might not put as much energy into his vocals as he used to but he owns each song and makes it work.

I purchased this via Amazon France the price was cheapest at that moment or seemed to be, doesn't matter since the item appears isposted from Korea!

This box appears to be a set designed for the Korean market, Korean translations are everywhere but not visible so inot "weird".

I was initially critical of its presentation, the box was extremely tight at first, tight enough to be a problem. It has loosened up without tearing so that is good. Another review on Amazon Germany mentioned precisely the same problem!

The individual discs are stored in as-nice-as-can-be replicas of the original jackets. I cannot comment on how closely the discs parallel the original issues or the masters used. The sound in all cases sounds as fine as is possible, is all I can say.

Milstein is interesting, largely forgotten by the general public (all it remembers is "Heifetz"), but on the evidence of this box, he had with Heifetz and Perlman, the largest stable of successful recordings of any violinist. The only other large box set of a violinist is Menuhin's, which is a compendium of many sources not just studio recordings and not just successful ones from his artistic peak. There may have been a Stern set at one time but it is no longer available. There has been no set that includes all or most of Oistrakh's recordings though he cries out for one

In contrast, this box doesn't have any discernable "stage" showing decline or even development. Every recording is perfect from any perspective. Progressive recordings of various great works may improve in aspects of their engineering but Milstein's playing is consistently stunning, beyond stunning.

I PERSONALLY find Mistein to be the "anti-Heifetz", an Auer pupil who preserved a warmth and sense of style his fellow student Mischa Elman had, and which Heifetz seems to have consciously purged his playing of. I have heard many recordings of Milstein, the ones that first captured my attention were his Columbias of baroque pieces. His adoption of those pieces in his repertoire was a big deal at the time and I find the same emotional depth in them that I would expect from a student of Enescu (for example) like Haendel. They are not included in this set but his virtues didn't change or diminish.

If you accept my characterization of Milstein Heifetz and Perlman as the only violinists with large "name-brand" sets devoted to their work, Milstein's box is an easy and mandatory choice, especially for people like myself who can't take Heifetz.

Getting past the easy characterization of Milstein as "immortal", and drilling down to details, I was struck how beautifully he played different styles of music, even across the great concertos, Tchaikovsky, Brahms, Beethoven, etc. Each sounds so "right" to me there isn't a moment when I longed to hear another favorite player. The same goes for the second tier concertos like the Saint-Saens.

I have to say, I did not expect to enjoy this set as much as I did, I bought it because I thought it was "required listening". A lovely set. It probably will become with the Callas "red box" and Horowitz Original Jacket, one of my most treasured boxed sets.
