review_title: Harnoncourt’s Four Seasons: not just the music of Vivaldi – the theatre of Vivaldi
review_text:
I never had this version in the LP era (or in the CD era until just now). The few excerpts I heard of it back then shocked me so much, went so much against my notions and expectations of how Spring should sound, that I kept it at bay, “vade retro Satanas”, for the next, well, decades. What I heard sounded to me like brutalized lines, arbitrary shifts of tempo, wayward phrasings. And obviously I wasn’t the only one to react that way. Among the critics of the time, there were those who were won over and raved upon it, and those who rejected it as repulsively as I did. Certainly the recording was controversial, even antagonizing – a trademark that Harnoncourt would probably have been proud of.

But then, little did I know back then – both figuratively and concretely. My expectations were shaped by the versions I knew, and these must have been Karajan’s first version with Michel Schwalbé and the Berlin Philharmonic (from 1972, [[ASIN:B000001G67 Four Seasons]]), and in the late 1970s or early 1980s, Jean-Claude Malgoire’s ([[ASIN:B000026I0Q Four Seasons, Violin Concertos]]) – like Harnoncourt’s one of the first on period instruments and released roughly at the same time.

In fact, Harnoncourt’s and Malgoire’s recordings were part of the earliest batch of Seasons recordings on period instruments. If I haven't missed anything, the very first recording on period instruments was Trevor Pinnock’s with his English Concerto for CRD, made May 1976, with the rest of the Opus 8 cycle recorded in April 77 ([[ASIN:B002NXSSPQ Vivaldi: Concertos, Op. 8 - The Four Seasons]]). The Four Seasons were first released individually, and reviewed in The Gramophone of November 1977; the rest came out a little less than a year later. Teldec/Warner also provides two recording dates for Harnoncourt, October 76 and March 77: I am supposing that the Seasons were recorded first, than the rest of the Opus 8 cycle. But Teldec originally published the complete cycle, and it was reviewed in The Gramophone of March 1978. Collegium Aureum followed, with a recording made in February 1977 ([[ASIN:B00002586S Vivaldi: Le Quattro Stagione (Four Seasons); La Tempesta di Mare; Il Piacere]], Gramophone review from October 1979). Malgoire was recorded in January 1978 and reviewed in The Gramophone of August. Kuijken and Petite Bande recorded their version in June 1979, [[ASIN:B00002470I Four Seasons: Oboe Concertos]].

And hearing these versions now, when so much has happened since on the front of Vivaldi interpretation, and now that I’ve listened to much, much more, score in hand, I discover how much and how radically my expectations have changed.

Vivaldi’s Four Seasons are famously introduced by four sonnets, one per season, of poor poetry but presumed to be from Vivaldi himself, and which give the underlying program of his four violin concertos, with direct and precise correspondences in the various episodes of the score. And when you read the successive verses under their respective place in the score, it becomes obvious how much Vivaldi’s Seasons are not just “music”, not even “evocative” music. They are descriptive music, even graphically descriptive music, and even more than that: they are theatre in music.

But, listening to all those versions, from the very first recording made in 1942 by Bernardo Molinari and the Rome Saint Cecilia Orchestra ([[ASIN:B0002N6T8M Four Seasons]]), to those of the 1970s and later, it is striking how so many of them seem to have given short shrift to the theatre in Vivaldi’s Seasons, and played them as if they were “just” music with no programmatic content. A listener without the score, sonnets and precise correspondence between verse and score would be hard put to recognize what the music was talking about. Sure, bird songs in the first movements of Spring and Summer, that’s pretty easy – although the cuckoo is not always recognizable in the first movement of Summer, not when tempo plods. Spring and summer storms maybe (not always recognizable, even them, at the plodding tempos adopted by many), soft winds of spring, flowing water-sources, winter chill.

But dog barking in the Largo of Spring, those gentle, elegant, almost inaudible punctuations of the viola? Swarms of horseflies and thunder in the Largo of Summer? Despaired shepherd meditating on his fate in the first movement of Summer? Inebriated villager in the first movement of Autumn and slumbering drunk villager at the end of the same? Joyful dances to greet spring or the autumn harvest in the two Allegros of Spring and the first movement of Autumn, at those laid-back to plodding tempos and with those thick string textures? Horse-riding huntsmen in the Finale of Autumn? (Riding heavy-hooved draft-horses, you mean… ) Gunshots, beast frantically running from hounds, and ultimately dying under their assault? Gushing winds, violently erupting storms? No, I don’t hear that in those versions. Just pretty music, that certainly expresses something (interpretation is open to the listener), but certainly not what Vivaldi’s sonnets describe.

So the historical AND musical significance of Harnoncourt’s recording was that he was the first ever to play not just the music, but the theatre, of Vivaldi’s Four Seasons. And his interpretation remains still entirely valid and up-to-date today.

His Allegros are lively, creating even, in the dancing Finale of Spring, an undercurrent of inquietude. The dance to rejoice at the autumn harvest is boisterous and romping. Summer storms erupt with shattering violence, and the foot-stamping in Winter (track 10) sounds like a winter storm. Harnoncourt sometimes favors extremes of tempo: I’ve never heard I think such a racing and vigorous hunt (Finale of Autumn) – now those are horses truly galloping, not just prancing, let alone the sturdy draft-horses many versions have turned them into, and gunshots really explode. On the other hand his opening of Summer is not the Allegro non molto Vivaldi’s score calls for, but a Lento, not doubt to evoke the feeling of languor under the crushing sun described by Vivaldi’s sonnet. But I appreciate that, in the Finale of Winter, in the short sirocco episode where that opening melody of Summer returns (1:56), he should relax only slightly his Allegro tempo and NOT follow the old and ungrounded tradition of playing it (without any indication of the score to that effect) much slower: sirocco in Italy is not a gentle breeze, but a wind that can be quite violent.

But it’s not just the visceral excitement of tempo and speed: it’s character. As soon as the first measures and tutti ritornello of Spring, Harnoncourt’s interpretation is filled with details and ideas of phrasing that are too numerous to describe, and always keep attention awake. The various bird calls in the first movements of Spring and Summer are played with great freedom of pulse, cadenza-like (it shocked me decades ago, it now sounds to me like the only valid way to phrase them, and the approach has been adopted by most performers today), although stereo separation could have been better in the bird trio of the first movement of Spring (0:28), as well as in the stormy Finale of Summer – here Vivaldi’s antiphonal exchanges between first and second violins aren’t clearly elucidated. The dog really barks in the Autumn Largo (funny to read the Vivaldi critic in Fanfare of November 1979, Niels Anderson, complaining of "the overly loud and distracting bass in the second movement of Spring”. Makes you wonder if he ever looked at the score, or if he understood Italian; Vivaldi instructs to play these dog barks "molto forte, a strappato", with a violent tearing movement of the bow...). In the Finale of Spring, I have heard no other version where the viola sounded, not just “as much as here”, but simply “as here”, like a bagpipe drone. In the first of Summer, the plaint of the villager (4:06) sounds like a real plaint, not just like a pretty melody without dramatic content. The episode of the beast’s death in the Finale of Autumn (1:58) is rendered splendidly, because Harnoncourt applies a dose of theatrical freedom to his racing tempo. Winter is suitably chilly (and in the opening of Winter Harnoncourt phrases, as written, by the quarter-note, not to the eighth-note as most performers).

Certainly, even I am ready to pick nit with some aspects and details of Harnoncourt’s rendition. The Finale of Spring could have been more sharply articulated, here the dance of nymphs and shepherds sounds a little too mushy-legato. The cuckoo in summer (first movement, track 4, 1:37) is high-strung, almost on cocaine, to the point that the actual cuckoo melody (it’s embedded in a figuration of rapid eighth-notes) might get lost to uninformed ears. I think there was plenty of scope to depict an even more inebriated peasant than what Alice Harnoncourt evokes in the opening Allegro of Autumn (0:58 track 7) – in fact, the only ones I know to have gotten this part right are Red Priest, in their transcription for flute, violin, cello and harpsichord, [[ASIN:B0000CERI1 Four Seasons]] – and I don’t exactly hear slumberous breathing in her phrasing of the penultimate episode in the same movement (3:04). In the Finale of Autumn, Harnoncourt’s very animated opening hunting tempo remains then too strict in the ensuing double-stops to really evoke the hunting horns they are evidently supposed to imitate (0:28) – that I think is a passage where Harnoncourt could have applied more cadenza-like freedom of pulse.

It’s easy also to take exception with some of Harnoncourt’s choices of tempo in the Largos: the Largo of Autumn flows, the shepherd’s sleep sounds agitated, not calm and appeased, and the undulating grass sounds more like a river rapidly flowing towards a cascade, or like time flying by with no return. As for the Largo of Winter, it is more than flowing, it is almost racing, and sure the violin pizzicatti are more in the direction of the pouring rain depicted by the sonnet than of the after-shower rain drops of most versions, but the solo violin melody doesn’t really evoke the cozy feelings of sitting by the fire – sounds more like very pressing wooing. But one is ready to accept a lot from a version with so much personality.

There was a point in the artistic history of the Harnoncourts when Nikolaus’ wife Alice seemed to have decided or accepted to step back in the shadow of her husband and act as his assistant in musicology and score preparation. But, on the evidence of these recordings, she was a violin virtuoso of the first order. The only thing that may mark out this version as being of its time is that she doesn’t add any ornamentation in the Largo of Spring – but she does in the Largo of Summer (there’s not much she can add in the racing Largo of Winter, and the slumbering Largo of Autumn is not one where the solo fiddler ornaments anyway). Harnoncourt alternates between organ and harpsichord as a continuo instrument. The organ provides more timbral homogeneity with the strings, but in the Largo of Autumn the harpsichord remains commendably discreet – in many versions it tends to become invasive, turning it into a harpsichord concerto of sorts, which is not the point.

I’ll return later to the other Opus 8 concertos. Even limited to The Four Seasons, this is, for both its historical importance and its musical validity still today, one of the main building blocks of any Vivaldi library. If it's only the Four Seasons you're interested in, check out the other editions of the same recording for best price, [[ASIN:B000000SL0 Vivaldi: The Four Seasons / Le Quattro Stagioni]], [[ASIN:B000000SQI Vivaldi - The Four Seasons (Le quattro stagioni) / Harnoncourt]], [[ASIN:B00004VKU1 Vivaldi: Four Seasons]]. For Harnoncourt's complete Opus 8, Warner's 2009 reissue is the edition I have: [[ASIN:B00277YJN8 Vivaldi: Il Cimento Dellarmonia E Dellinventione]].

review_title: Reflections in the prism of rippling water
review_text:
I don’t usually buy CDs of Jazz – it’s the “Satie” part that attracted me here. These compositions – most by founder and leader of the Vienna Art Orchestra Mathias Rüegg – are less “arrangements” of Satie than “inspirations from” Satie – Rüegg calls them “Reflections on” and, yes, that’s what they are, in both senses and, in meaning # 2 (“the act of reflecting, as in casting back a light or heat, mirroring, or giving back or showing an image; the state of being reflected in this way”), provided you consider that the mirror is a distorting one, or the reflection, one in the prism of rippling water. In many cases I don’t even get the core Satie cell, through lack of familiarity with the original pieces (tracks 1 to 4, based on the three pieces from the “Avant-Dernières Pensées” collection, and Sévère Réprimande” from “Véritables Préludes Flasques”) – but, checking on the scores, sure, the root is there, oftentimes the compositions start with what is indeed an arrangement of the Satie piece, but when that is stated, they take flight. The third Gnossienne, track 5, is even only that, an orchestration with a few added syncopations in the accompanying chords.

But the point is: the program is very enjoyable without making any reference to its Satiesque origin. Instrumentation is skillfully and entertainingly varied from composition to composition – prominent trombone then flute in the first, voice and metal percussion with underpinning of brass followed by solo trumpet in 2, tuba (or is it trombone?) and bells then solo soprano sax in 3, various metal percussion including, I think, vibraphone, and softly whispering flute in 4 soon joined by soprano (singer) playing in unison with various winds etc. The three Vexations, tracks 9-11 – the only tracks not credited to Mathias Rüegg - are improvisations, respectively for tenor sax, voice, and bass clarinet, over the terse and brooding ostinato bass line (played by vibraphone) of the famous obsessively repetitive piece of Satie (premiered, we are told, by John Cage and a group of pianists in 1963, in an 18-hour long concert), and the result is suitably obsessive, and strangely fascinating. The soloists are virtuosic and hugely exciting – soprano Lauren Newton’s scatting vocalizes in tracks 2 and 10 makes you wish for more (and her singing in unison with the wind instruments in various tracks is also quite beautiful), and Karl Fian’s trumpet in 2 is hilariously insane. Is it even Jazz? Sure, the saxophone, trumpet, brass combo point to Jazz and some moments are distinctly Jazzy. But some others, and other instrumental combinations, are closer to some forms of contemporary classical. Jazz is a vast territory.

Why Satie? According to the elaborate liner notes by famed Vienna composer HK Gruber, because Satie refused to distinguish between “high-browed” music and popular music – or rather, he did, by rejecting what was accepted in his time as “art music” and by elevating popular and other “low-browed” music to the status of art. “Jazz – by now an emancipated musical form – returns the sympathies of “Monsieur le Pauvre”, the (nick-)name Satie liked to give himself, and in its turn makes use of the composer’s ideas for its own innovations”. Also because of Satie’s utter rejection of psychology, sentimentalism and even sentiment in music, his creation of a “musique d’ameublement”, a notion wwhich the liner notes inaccurately translate into “furniture music”, but it goes way beyond, because there is a figurative meaning to the verb “meubler” in French, not just to fill with furniture, but to fill any void, any emptiness (especially silence) with a presence of something that is is little more than a semblance, a make-believe, but in truth even emptier than the emptiness that it is meant to fill. It is used very much with silence being filled by idle chatter, and it’s a notion actors use, when one of them forgets his lines. So “musique d’ameublement” could very well be translated by “music to hide silence under the carpet”.

The Vienna Arts Orchestra was a prominent Austrian Jazz Ensemble, founded in 1977 by Mathias Rüegg and, after various tribulations, changes of personel and size, terminally disbanded in 2010, whose core performers were saxophonists Wolfgang Puschnig and Harry Sokal, singer Lauren Newton, and tuba player Jon Sass. This recording was one of the ensemble’s, and of the Swiss label Hat Art’s, most popular successes. It first came out in 1984 as a double LP, hat ART 2005, and was issued to CD on CD 6024 in 1989. Bizarrely it’s been reissued twice on hat ART’s series Hatology, 560 (in 2001, [[ASIN:B00005MH94 The Minimalism of Erik Satie]], ASIN B00005MH94) and 671 (in 2008, [[ASIN:B0044ZQ8R6 Minimalism of Erik Satie]] ASIN B0044ZQ8R6). Why did they not simply re-press 560, don’t ask me. Buyers, beware: Amazon has automatically linked the three entries, the one for the original CD issue, CD 6024, and the two on Hatology, so that the reviews published under one will automatically appear under the two others. The one I have and which I am reviewing is the original issue, and if for some reason this is the edition you want, you will find it under ASIN B000025YVO, [[ASIN:B000025YVO The Minimalism of Erik Satie]]. Be careful when you click on the offers, the link might lead you to the other entries and editions. I assume, but don’t know for sure, that the elaborate presentation by HK Gruber has been reproduced in the two reissues. TT 75:14

review_title: A perfect blend of bluegrass and sacred steel
review_text:
Some guitar duets don't work because the guitarists are just too similar to make it worth anything. Others just can't find similar ground. Then, there are the perfect meetings. This is one of those.

I admit freely that I came to this album almost purely for Roosevelt Collier. Now, I love both bluegrass and sacred steel. However, Hall wasn't the attraction for me. I don't mind the Stringdusters, but they don't stand out enough from the crowd for me. Dobro has what I sometimes call an Art Tatum problem. Art Tatum was so astonishingly virtuosic on the piano that nobody could touch him. Advancing the instrument required looking for new concepts rather than trying to outplay him because, frankly, nobody would ever be able to do that. So, it took players like McCoy Tyner and Bill Evans to find conceptual approaches to advance the instrument. (Yes, and many in between, like Monk-- I'm not trying to write a complete history of the piano. I'm just making an analogy.) For the dobro, that player is, of course, Jerry Douglas. He is just so far beyond everyone else in technique that nobody can touch him. MAYBE Rob Ickes, but Flux is just such a virtuoso that the instrument has sort of stagnated as people try to catch up to him. The interesting dobro players are the ones who look for other approaches, like Billy Cardine, of The Biscuit Burners.

So, Andy Hall wasn't the attraction for me. Roosevelt Collier, though... If you follow sacred steel, you know him. He has been creeping around in the background for a few years, but without much recorded output. Go on youtube, though, and WOW is that guy amazing. So, I've been waiting for some Roosevelt Collier recordings. Honestly, I was hoping for some straight-up sacred steel, but whatever it was, I was going to get it.

Now, this could have been a train wreck. Instead, it was perfection on... Reuben's Train. That old bluegrass standard wound up being the perfect meeting ground for a bluegrass honcho and a sacred steel virtuoso to blend their styles, which are both rooted in blues and gospel anyway. These two listen to each other and learn from each other. That is what should happen on this kind of album, and when the styles have common roots anyway, that's when you have the potential for real magic.

I point out Reuben's Train for special mention here because some of the other tracks lean either more towards bluegrass or more towards sacred steel, but finding a proper blend is hard. Nevertheless, Roosevelt Collier and Andy Hall are always listening to each other, always searching for common ground, and playing their rear-ends off. I knew I was a Roosevelt Collier fan, and now I'm an Andy Hall fan too. I don't know if I'll go out and get any Stringdusters albums since they tend to play their bluegrass a bit too straight for my tastes these days, but I hope to hear more from Andy as he experiments more.

review_title: One of the finest prog albums I've heard from Spain
review_text:
Mezquita was a prog rock band from Córdoba, Spain that coughed up two albums, Recuerdos de mi Tierra in 1979 and Califas del Rock in 1981, both on the Chapa label (same label that brought you Crack's Si Todo Hiciera). Much of their reputation lies on their debut. It's hard to believe that such great prog would come out in 1979 (it's well known how badly many British prog bands were doing at this time), but Recuerdos de mi Tierra is perhaps one of the finest albums from 1979 I've ever heard, in fact one of the finest prog rock albums from Spain ever! Do you like Triana, but wish there was more punch and energy? Mezquita delivers, and delivers big time! This is some highly energetic flamenco prog with some incredible performance from all around. They tend to use a lot of scales used in both flamenco and Middle Eastern/North African music. Keyboards including Hammond organ and Moog, maybe a little Mellotron (I think I hear some tron strings and odd choir sound that don't sound like your standard tron choir, much like what I heard from Shylock's "Choral" off Ile de Fievre), although real strings are used on many of the cuts (four guys are credited to strings). Vocals are all in Spanish, and remind me a bit of Triana's Jesús de la Rosa. I really like how the guitars (from José Rafa) compete with the rest of the music. Roska's keyboard work is very much integrated into the music, but still obviously easily noticed. It's one of those albums it's really difficult to pick out the highlights, so I won't.

Of course such albums are difficult to come by as an original LP, but Si-Wan in Korea had reissued this on CD, as well as (more recently) Picar in Spain, who retained the original cover artwork, but changed the "Mezquita" typefont (I guess they did that to make it more easily readable, but I had no problem reading the original typefont found on the original LP or the Si-Wan CD). I own the Picar reissue.

Don't you love it when you find great prog and it was released after 1977/'78? This is one of them, and it's without a doubt a completely essential album!

review_title: No Period Instruments, no Historically Informed Performance Practice, just excellent Haydn
review_text:
These recordings were issued as Erato Records LPs in 1966 and 1967. In 1988 they were reissued on this Erato CD, which is ADD (analog recording, digital mixing, digital transfer). There were a lot of bad digital transfers in the 1980s, but this is a good one. It was part of Erato's "Collection Bonsai," budget reissues of their 20+ year-old back catalog.

In his salad days in the 1960s, Austrian conductor Theodor Guschlbauer recorded Haydn, Mozart and Schubert for Erato Records with the Bamberg Symphony and the Vienna Baroque Ensemble. I had never heard of the later group, the orchestra in this recording. They do not sound like a modern baroque ensemble. They sound like the English Chamber Orchestra and the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields back in the 1960s, and if you enjoy those historic recordings, you should investigate this one.

Theodor Guschlbauer trained as a cellist and studied conducting with Hans Swarowsky, Lovro von Matačić and Herbert von Karajan. He became music director of the Lyon Opera in 1969 and general music director of the Linz Bruckner Orchestra in 1975. He was not a disciple of Historically Informed Performance, but he did not try to make Haydn sound like Bruckner.

Symphony No. 53 was the most popular of Haydn's symphonies before 1779, when Haydn's music belonged to the Esterházy family and all of his published music was pirated. Symphony No. 77 is one of three written for a 1782 English concert tour that fell through. Symphony No. 61 is another symphonic high point from the 1770s and an earlier work than No. 53. All three symphonies are delightful in these fine recorded performances.

Warner Music should reissue this but I doubt they ever will. It is not a collectors' item, and it is well worth $8 or $9 for a clean used copy.

If you love Doo Wop but are tired of hearing "Earth Angel" one more time, this CD will be a breath of fresh air. This great CD is not the same old tired stuff. If you are looking for familiar tunes to jostle old memories, go elsewhere. These groups may be familiar, but the songs are not their old recordings. Here's the story:

In the mid 80s, Marty Pekar produced seven Doo Wop albums for Epic under a subsidiary name, Ambient Records. He rounded up the best, still-performing, vocal groups from the 50s and 60s and recorded new music in the exact style of their original hits. The goal was not to produce new hits, but to revitalize a musical style that was his personal favorite, and perhaps introduce a younger generation to this great genre.

The Capris, whose "There's a Moon Out Tonight" was a hit in 1958, actually charted with "Morse Code of Love" in 1983. The song was covered by the Manhattan Transfer in 1985. This song is so perfectly 50s, it's hard to believe it was recorded in the 80s.

Grab one up while they're still available, and it's great to see Intrada getting hold of wonderful Paramount scoring sessions like this one.

In 1950 Sir Thomas, then a spry 71, toured his recently formed (1946) RPO through North America and South Africa, and the dirigent and his handpicked orchestra were newly signed to the Dutch imprint Philips, also dating from 1950. Columbia Masterworks repressed the Beecham/RPO Philips discography in mass quantities for the North American market, and Beecham made quite outstanding sets of his specialties in Berlioz (overtures, HAROLD EN ITALIE, TE DEUM) and Delius (SEA DRIFT, HASSAN, MASS OF LIFE, et al.), duly reissued in digital resequencings by Sony.

This is a more dullish (mostly late 18th century) set, from its drab cover art to routine performances of the Beethoven, Brahms and Boccherini (Beecham had those three B-composers in his standing repertoire, pointedly excluding Bach) overtures. The French items—each anticipating Beecham’s highly esteemed Berlioz—are far less routine, and the lengthy CHASSE DE JEUNE HENRI (more a symphonic poem than overture) is really exciting, with the whooping RPO brass (including Dennis Brain) imitating hunting horns and Sir Tommy reveling in the orchestral drama of a woodland chase (see too Beecham’s indispensable EMI recordings of hunt music in Berlioz’ “Royal hunt and storm” ex-LES TROYENS or Haydn’s autumnal tally-ho episode in THE SEASONS).

The B-composers are downers in this programme, but the French items directly predate and prefigure Beecham’s rather more sparkling EMI stereo sets LOLLIPOPS (in two volumes), BONBONS and FAVOURITE OVERTURES, and the stylish Méhul items are really essential for dedicated Beechamites. My copy of this set (ML 5029) evidently dates from 1955, a Columbia “six-eye” pressing that is deep-grooved, proudly unbreakable and built to last, reproducing the Philips masters with honest mono resonance. Modern collectors will find the stunning Méhul performances digitally reissued as filler for the impassioned William Primrose/Beecham/RPO recording of HAROLD EN ITALIE in Sony’s SIR THOMAS BEECHAM CONDUCTS series.

review_title: ON THE DANUBE: LEHAR AT HOME IN BUDA-PESTH
review_text:
Smart discophiles would routinely ignore this sow's ear of a CD, presented so generically and inexpensively that it resembles a shameful secret dragged from the depths of the Laserlight (their series MASTERS OF CLASSICAL MUSIC: LEHAR samples six of these 11 tracks) or Naxos backlists, fit for classical newbies only and then fated to flea-market CD extinction. I'd been listening to Istvan Kertesz and Franz Lehar (as conductor) latterly, and mindful that the most sparkling and lilting Lehar recordings always came from Vienna (or Zurich) I was curious to hear what Lehar's countrymen downstream on the Danube were doing with (or to) his music. I specifically sought a Magyar conductor and a Magyar band for completely alamode Lehar and, buying on spec, I found a real bonanza for Lehar specialists like myself.

On offer here, cunningly masked as an undesirable orphan CD, is an integral rerelease of a mainstream 1977 Qualiton album, originally titled GOLD UND SILBER: ORCHESTRAL HITS. I found a silken purse, an unfamiliar and interesting maestro, idiomatically suave Lehar standards and in the bonus tracks a super Danubian sleeper. The Lehar hits are a predictable overture/waltz selection, but the performances by Janos Sandor and the Budapest Philharmonic are ideal, ablaze with color and striking rhythmic elasticity (the Budapest rubato is more daring than the Viennese). Sandor programs the standalone concert-waltz masterpiece GOLD UND SILBER as well as rarer selections from FRASQUITA and EVA, and in the PAGANINI extract there's a stellar violin solo played by Istvan Tamas. These performances are so wholly within the authentic Lehar idiom that I rank them alongside the reference standards conducted by Paulik, Boskovsky and Lehar himself. Sandor (1933-2010), it turns out, was born to do this. He conducted and recorded extensively in both Gyor and Budapest, specializing in Bartok and Mahler, but also preferring--like Lehar--lighter, martial and occasional music. He emigrated to Canada in 1991 and was particularly active in Victoria, Edmonton and Banff with youth and collegiate orchestras.

In the brief bonus tracks the more familiar Maestro Janos (Ferencsik, 1907-84) conducts the Hungarian State Orchestra in three dance excerpts by Delibes, Strauss fils and Lanner, with the Strauss polka ELJEN A MAGYAR! just fizzing along and the Lanner Danubian discovery PESTH-WALZER having great Rakoczy-style bugle calls.

As a Lehar specialist I'm completely surprised by and smitten with this unassuming release, and I'll recommend it too to general listeners who need reminding that there's more than one great musical capital on the banks of the muddy brown Danube.

review_title: An Excellent Rendition of Berlioz's Requiem
review_text:
The Requiem Op.5 is one of Berlioz's greatest works and its performance demands luxuriously a large scale orchestra, a boys' choir, a huge chorus and a tenor (in IX Sanctus). The array is no less enormous than Mahler's symphony No.8 requires.

Simply speaking, Sir Colin Davis and LSO ensure an excellent Berlioz performance. This splendid Requiem recording of 1969, like other Berlioz discs from LSO under the baton of Davis, can be rated first class in terms of all aspects. Davis's unique reading is as charming as before, especially at chorus sections. The original recording keeps high level of Philips and the CD transfer is also well done.

Colin Davis ranks absolutely among greatest Berlioz exponents. This Requiem interpretation stands undoubtedly along with those legendary performances from Charles Munch and Sir Thomas Beecham.

Highly recommended!

review_title: Rare but worthy memorial to an outstanding musician
review_text:
How very sad that the late John Toll (1947-2001) didn't make more solo recordings. This is the only one I can trace, and it's stunning. But Orlando Gibbons was a great choice for demonstrating Toll's abilities. For the composer was a Tudor musician of the first order, brilliant, versatile and profound, and there isn't a single one of his works, secular or sacred, that doesn't have something to say.

The present disc is a collection of his keyboard works, some of them played on the harpsichord and some on the organ. Both instruments are superb – the harpsichord a modern copy of a 1637 Ruckers, the organ the 1693 instrument in Adlington Hall, Cheshire. Both are ideally suited to this music. John Toll has a terrific way with the keyboard, playing with seemingly natural style, energy and insight in every one of these works. There are twenty-four pieces here, a representative selection of the various forms of Gibbons' works including Prelude, Fantasia, Pavan, Galliard, and including one of my particular favourites, the Italian Ground (track 22); this latter, while not so reflective or profound as some of the other pieces, nevertheless epitomises the distinctive quality and mastery of melody characteristic of the Tudor era. The disc's evocative title is named after another of the works, The Woods so Wild (3). The programme concludes with an especially inspired and energetic piece, Fantasia for Double Organ – even if its title is not to be taken literally.

My only reservation stems from a habitual irritation over recitals in which we are switched back and forth several times from one instrument to another – in the present case, harpsichord and organ. Still, at least we don't get a virginal or several other instruments as well, so I suppose two aren't bad; what is more, the choice for each work is invariably appropriate and the recordings, although actually made in two different places, are of outstanding quality, beautifully matched and conveying an entirely consistent ambience. Booklet notes by Andrew Parker are extremely useful and interesting, and there's also a tribute to the player from John Holloway.

I might have been tempted to deprive this disc of one star in the above rating because of my own personal reaction to the musical-chairs approach. However, that would not adequately reflect either the beauty of Gibbons' music, the player's superb interpretations, or my respect for an outstanding performer who is no longer with us. Altogether this is an exceptionally fine representation, not only of John Toll's abilities but of the keyboard music of a great composer.

review_title: A great indie/private press country rock album from 1973 by a Canadian Lamanite band in Nashville
review_text:
Billy Thunderkloud & the Chieftones, ALL THROUGH THE NIGHT, Superior Records SR 103. Vinyl Lp.

Back cover lists Buddy Lee Management, Attractions Inc., while the label producer credit states "Produced by Duane Allen." The record label shows a 1973 date, flat silver-grey label with black printing, while the album cover states 1974. This appears/sounds to be a professional recording, but a private press indie, with "Indi/Kloud Productions, LTD" in the top right of the front cover. I've seen Billy Thunderkloud's albums around, usually filed with '70s rock acts, and found some nice ones to satisfy my vinyl junkie curiosity while flipping through BYU's LAMANITE GENERATION [[ASIN:B00YTWM7H4 Lamanite Generation]], BYU's YOUNG AMBASSADORS pop covers' private press Lps, Arliene Nofchissey's Lps with Stan Bronson and a Chief Dan George [[ASIN:B00BJDODKK Proud Earth- Chief Dan George - LP (1975)]] on a Provo, Utah label, and the usual assortment of Mario Lanza casino lounge RCA albums by Utah/Las Vegas crooner Rouvann. It surprised to see Nashville credits on Billy Thunderkloud's work. My copy sports an autograph to "Judd" in pen, too! This was a working band, and GOOD, too!

side one--

side two--

Sound is stereo, Vocals, drums, bass centered. Alternating on either speaker are electric and acoustic guitar(s), flute, piano left, horns and a gospel piano sound on "Testament," and an uncredited but very obvious female backing vocal group on all tracks. Style on the Lp runs from early '70s Elvis country, with more than a hint of Conway Twitty, Charlie Rich, and a rockier Waylon Jennings vocal feeling. Songs: "Battle Hymn of the Republic" is a definite nod to Elvis. "Little Arrows" was a Leapy Lee hit on Decca, and "Running Bear" dates back to 1960, but I think the version here follows Sonny James's country hit on Capitol. Of the three Lps I have on Billy Thunkerkloud, this is the most rock-y sounding; the two 20th Century Lps are solidly country, though the best of them the first, OFF THE RESERVATION.

review_title: Strange, strange, strange, strange...even more strange
review_text:
The idea of this album is off the meter. -- April, 1968

You might imagine, in the aftermath of the Beatles' SGT. PEPPER Lp the year before, if Pat Boone ...or Lawrence Welk... had sponsored his version of the Mamas & the Papas, then whitewashed Motown soul. Stylistically, this album more than suggests the Mike Curb Congregation's WALT DISNEY'S GREATEST HITS a few years later. Smiley-happy, white vacant amusement park interchangable employees happily singing more-than-vanilla versions of Motown catalog.

It's a short package--10 songs, even for a period Lp. Normally Columbia pop albums had 11 tracks when this package issued, which suggests that this album was shorted one song, mostly likely to cut down on the mechanical royalty payments due for Barry Gordy's song catalog. Track list:

Side one--
Dancing in the Streets/Where Did Our Love Go/Reach Out (I'll Be There)/Stop in the Name of Love/Ain't Gonna Waste My Time
Side two--
Shotgun/Ain't No Mountain High Enough/My Girl/A Place in the Sun/Just Look at Her Now

"Where Did Our Love Go," "Stop in the Name of Love," and "A Place in the Sun" are treated as dreamy slow ballads, a la what the Doodletown Pipers did to the Beatles' "A Hard Day's Night," and the Christies' own execreble slow version of "I Want to Hold Your Hand" on their NEW KICK album a little before. The male group vocals on "My Girl" wreaks of earnestness. "Ain't No Mountain High Enough" is also slowed down, and the lead male vocal just calls out a vocal presence resembling Conway Twitty, if he'd crooned lounge. The album ends with a comic reading (ugh) version of "Just Look At Her Now," complete with "wah-wah-wah..." alto sax and muted trumpet aping laughing, and guitar with a "wah-wah" pedal. Overall, the band and backing on this set sounds like the house band for an early '70s variety/music TV show like those by Tony Orlando & Dawn, Jim Nabors, etc...--not quite right funky bass and rock guitar, too loud horn section over-weighed by trumpets blasting away, add the occasional harpsicord, orchestra string section, just oozing "This is SHOW BUSINESS!!!"

From the late '60s, this is one of three albums Columbia and affiliated acts don't seem to want remembered/reissued: The Brothers Four, THE LENNON-MCCARTNEY SONGBOOK, and Tony Bennett, SINGS THE GREAT HITS OF TODAY.

Kitsch recommended!

That song needed editing and gets very repetitive, but it isn't a terrible sound.  The other 5 instrumentals are in the mold of Pink Floyd, as is the entire CD.  If you like Pink Floyd, you'll like this CD which is 43 minutes and 39 seconds long. In fact if you like Pink Floyd you will probably be sorry you don't have this CD.  Of course it is obscure and will probably never be heard much in the U.S.  But give it a try and you will not be sorry.

I discovered this CD back in 1993, when I was living in Japan, through a music magazine...well, it was half of this CD. I had found a mail-in offer for a seven song acoustic set from: The Allman Brothers Band, live in Los Angeles. Acoustic Allman Brothers? Yeah, count me in on this!

Well, that short seven track CD of live Allmans with acoustic guitars, quickly became one of my favorite discs. This updated version adds a seven song acoustic set from Amy Ray & Emily Saliers, known to the world as The Indigo Girls, and doubles the length of the CD to 69 minutes.

The live set of The Indigo Girls is outstanding. At the time of this show at the Radio & Records Convention on: 06/11/92, the girls had been touring to support their recent release: "Rites Of Passage." The sound of this show is amazing, as if the Indigo Girls are playing in your living room. With two guitars and two voices, these great songs: "Joking", "Welcome Me", "Ghost", "Galileo", "The Water Is Wide", "Three Hits" and that big Hit: "Closer To Fine" have never sounded better. 5-Stars for The Indigo Girls half of this CD.

The Allman Brothers, have never released an official live acoustical record, so this half of the CD is very unique. From the opener: "Come On In My Kitchen" throught to the closing chords of: "Melissa", its all bright and crisp, as versions of: "In Memory Of Elizabeth Reed" and "Seven Turns" have a wonderful sound clarity, new life is brought onto these old favorites. Gregg, sounds like he had a home in a Mississippi cotton field in 1932. Dickey Betts, is always relaxed in an acoustic setting, and on this, he is at his best.

The Allmans, are a full band for this performance, and even un-plugged, they are still a force to behold. "Midnight Rider" is one of their best, and this is the best live version that I have heard. The lead guitars of Warren and Dickey, play of each other as only string wizards are able to accomplish. I loved this CD in 1993, and it has doubled in greatness, with the addition of Amy & Emily's set added on.

This is a Five-Star CD... but, I have lowered the rating to: Four-Stars, because it is so rare and so hard to find, and if you do locate this, you are going to have to bring in a bag of gold to equal the purchase price.
This CD needs to be released officially by the record corporations, it is too good to hide from the music fans any longer!

"Just Piano 2" is the second in a series of original solo piano recordings from British pianist/composer Kerry Barnes. Self-taught from an early age until she was in her late teens, Barnes went on to pass her Grade 7 and 8 Music Exams in a period of four months, and later earned several composing certifications as well. She now composes music for the Board Exams as well as for her own recordings and sheet music. More than 20 years ago, Barnes was diagnosed with Focal Dystonia, an incurable neurological condition that primarily affects the hands and fingers. It manifests itself by causing complete incoordination, and is also very painful. Given those limitations, it is more than impressive that Barnes continues to be driven to create and share her music. Although she works within a collection of basic patterns that her brain will allow her to play, Barnes’ music is not repetitive or simplistic. She has done extensive studies of Russian classical music and some of those influences are apparent in her original work. Just Piano 2 is dedicated to the memory of Barnes’ sister, Jane, who passed away last year from cancer. The music on the album ranges from bright and playful to expressing grief, and most of the sixteen pieces are classically structured and very melodic; they are also very expressive and colorful.

"Just Piano 2" begins with “Pastures New,” a piece with a gracefully flowing left hand and a lovely, bittersweet melody that builds to a passionate middle section and then returns to the original melody - a beautiful start! “Latinopia” takes on a smoldering, exotic flavor that is quite different from Barnes’ other music - I like it! “Polish Dance” hints of Chopin’s elegance and emotional power without getting into his finger-twisting intricacies. “Sister’s Lament” was played at Kerry’s sister’s funeral, and although sadness is the underlying emotion, I sense many happy memories were interwoven throughout the piece. “Circles 2” is much more playful and carefree. “Perpetual Motion” is a favorite. Moving constantly, with frequent changes from major to minor keys and some effective deep bass accents that reverberate from the low end of the piano, it’s a fascinating study. “Christine” is a gorgeous expression of love from deep within. Graceful and very sincere, it’s a beauty! “Floral Notes” is so simple and so spare, but touches the heart with its honesty and openness. As the title suggests, “Poem Melancholia” is not about a happy experience, but the piece isn’t without hope. The last track is called “Just a Minute” and lasts for all of 51 seconds, ending the album playfully and with a grin.

What a happy discovery Kerry Barnes and her music have been! I have thoroughly enjoyed both "Just Piano" and "Just Piano 2," and look forward to hearing more of what Ms Barnes has to offer! Check it out!

Isabel Allende gave the world a wonderful origin story for the legend of Zorro. Yes, I grew up with the black and white TV show and have enjoyed the various movies. But this story was the first tale that gave Zorro true seriousness. This tale opens in the 1790s with the meeting of Diego de la Vega's parents, Alejandro de la Vega and Toypurnia (a warrior for one of the local Native American tribes). Toypurnia is injured in an attack on Padre Mendoza's mission and while recuperating, Alejandro befriends her. Toypurnia becomes a lady in waiting to a family friend of the de la Vegas and is renamed Regina. Shortly thereafter, Alejandro proposes marriage.

This riveting tale continues on from there with the birth of Diego and his antics as a boy. His milk brother (so called because they were both breast fed by the same woman) Bernado, a full blooded Native American, was born in the same week. An antic with a bear particularly stood out for me. The book then takes a more serious turn when pirates attack this California coastal village, leaving a few dead and many scarred for life. As Diego and Bernado become young men, they have an opportunity to go off to Catalan-speaking Spain to allow Diego to polish off his schooling. The antics continue, including performance in a gypsy circus, sword-training by a master of a secret society, and young love. While I won't spoil anymore of the plot line, just know there are plenty more surprises in store in this book as Diego and Bernado make their way back to California.

Of the three, this is by far the best, not only meeting but far exceeding my expectations. One can hear the incredible resonance of this chamber, a resonance that has often been described as the echo of the universe, clearly & distinctly (both aurally and morally, if you will).  Even though the fans of easy listening may not enjoy this (because they do not understand what they are actually hearing), this is a MONUMENTAL ethnomusicological document.  Anyone who values any of the deeper mystical layers of music, or the basic historical & anthropological value of it should be immensely satisfied with their purchase. review_text:
Following their successful work projects on their Debut Album and on the Hokuto No Ken Anime Series, The group Tom Cat offered to the public a second album.

Fence.

A release of five songs. Among them the main title Fence; my favourite release out of this record. A song of emotion that just catches your heart and refuses to let you go. One of the best melodies released from this J-Rock Group.

Another tune I loved as well was So What?; the Instrumental intro as it presented each group member and made us realise the good camaraderie that exists among everyone. Even better was when they played with the sound display of their group as if you listen with headphones, they play music one moment on the right side, then to the left one.

So in terms of music, always a beautiful job from this group. Though my only criticism would be that I wish they could have released more songs as this group is excellent. I even felt they could have also put their Tough Boy and Love Song from the Hokuto No Ken Anime in it as well. But maybe they couldn’t or they had already released them in another record destined only for the anime series Soundtrack.

Either way, the album is another beautiful display of Rock music. And if you check inside the CD, you get a poster that offers on one side a photo of the main Singer, and behind all the songs’ lyrics.

As for the Cd’s recording quality, the engineering is top notch. The volumes are well balanced and we do not hear any parasite noises during the listening. Kudos to the whole team behind that work people tend to forget to thank for were it not for that team, then any group’s music would be non-listenable.

In sum, the album Fence is a great purchase for the group’s fans. Though I still find it sad that they haven’t released further CDs than this one as I find them more talented than other groups that are over-promoted in the worldwide medias and whose music/lyrics pale in comparison to what Tom Cat give to the public.

Listening to the Xenosaga Episode III soundtrack makes me realize that I perhaps judged the previous soundtrack too harshly. While this installment has a more refined feel and sound to it than its predecessor, I can't help but to feel that Xenosaga II actually has the more memorable tracks. Ms. Kajiura obviously feels the same way as she reuses a number of tunes from her previous contribution to the series. Hepatica, especially #2 sounds like a reworked Sweet Song, Promised Pain is what Communication Breakdown would have been had the song continued, A New World sounds very similar to I am Free, She's Coming Back is Here she Comes, and Fate is Fatal Fight. She even borrows from Madlax with Godsibb sounding like If I Die from the OST 2. Although not very creative or imaginative it doesn't necessarily make for a bad soundtrack. While there were some tracks that are well done there are just as many others that are completely forgettable. In fact most of the tracks blended into the next one making me completely forget what the one before it sounded like. The average tracks such as Dark omen, Creeping into, Zarathustra Dungeon, and Shifting Territories, the last two in spite of the different names and separate track listings actually being the same song, weigh down those that were actually well done with both Febronias, Hepatica (Kos-Mos), and Promised Pain being among the latter. Rolling down the UMN is also noteworthy, it's a nice jazz arrangement which is a welcome change from Yuki's typical fare, yet it's completely out of place here. We've Got to Believe in Something is also enjoyable although during the duration of the song I'm constantly trying to remember what other song it reminds me of.

The average and the exceptional are so intertwined however, that it gives the soundtrack an uneven inconsistent feel to it, and nowhere is that inconsistency more obvious than in the vocal track. Maybe Tomorrow is by far one of the most uninspired, generic, ill arranged vocal tracks that I've had the misfortune of hearing. It's disheartening and disappointing to know that Maybe Tomorrow is the song that that the Xenosaga series will end on. I had hoped for something memorable and lasting, yet instead I am left with something that sounds like a hidden track on a Kidz Bop CD.

Disappointing ending theme aside, as a whole the soundtrack isn't bad. While not offering anything of substance it is best described as aural bubblegum, enjoyable for the time and yet completely forgettable once the song is over. Fans of Ms. Kajiura's work will love it, people who are only vaguely familiar with her work will like it, and those who have heard anything by her before and weren't overwhelmed with it will be hit with a sense of deja vu that may border on rehash. While I hesitate to call it great, it's still above average and is worth giving a listen to.

No reviews..probably few people know who or what this cd release is about so I will share my limited exposure(I just recently purchased this!).
First off this is mid 90s electronic music a nice balance of some down-tempo acid based tracks wrapped within semi ambient blippy material.
Dandy Jack released a few albums/cds on the Rather Interesting label which I believe was owned or operated by genius electronic maestro Atom Heart(Uwe Schmidt) loosely associated with Fax Germany(now defunct RIP Mr. Namlook!).
The opening track is a smooth operator combining chime laden synths with repetitive bass-lines motifs, arpeggiated notes and all supported by 4/4 kick. There is plenty of variation on this disc and nothing is really too monotonous, Jack tends to keep it "rather interesting". Other tracks can be a little more aggressive but nothing like the really hard techno that was spilling out of Belgium and Germany during the same time period.
If you enjoy your music downtempo and in and of the classic 90s era European landscape this should suite your listening venue quite apply.

A child prodigy, Ernst Wilhelm Wolf (1735-1792) was born near Gotha in Germany. Once CPE Bach heard some of his compositions, they developed a live long friendship. Known for his vocal works, Wolf also wrote instrumental music, at least 35 symphonies, many keyboard compositions, and 12 surviving string quartets. Three of the 5 quartets on this recording are from his Op.3 set, published in 1785.

Written in B Flat, the first quartet begins with a moderately paced intro. After a striking unison phrase, the schizophrenic ‘Allegro assai’ kicks into high gear with the 1st violin leading the charge. Amid scurrying violins, rolling triplets from the viola, a bravura solo emerges in the bass line. Interspersed with more contemplative interludes, the unison phrase returns periodically to energize this marvelous opening movement. Shifting into F Minor for the following ’Adagio’, Wolf plumbs the depths of despair, again employing the lower strings in vital roles. Listen for a splendid cello passage in the very deepest register of the instrument. A merry ‘Allegro con spirito’ concludes the quartet with busy finger work from all four voices.

Dark and foreboding, the initial theme of the moody ‘Allegro assai’ of the G Minor Quartet, Op.3, No.3 is presented by the lead voice, then developed by all. Characterized by adept contrapuntal writing, the tone brightens and then reverses as the key changes from minor to major, and then, sometimes within a measure or two. Offering a graceful respite, the G Major ‘Andantino’ is a triple metered contrast to the stormy outer movements. Bursting from the silence between tracks, furious fiddling drives the agitated ‘Allegro piu tosto presto’ to a terrific finale, with a sudden stillness echoing after the last notes.

Unpublished during Wolf’s lifetime, the Quartet in C Major likely was written in 1789, and may have been his last. The measured ‘Allegretto’ features sharply delineated counterpoint with the viola assuming high prominence as it jousts with the upper strings. Opening in an ominous C Minor, the ensuing ‘Largo’ slides into E Flat as this pensive 2nd movement unfolds. With the viola again taking a solo turn, it reverts to minor and drifts to a somber close. Light and lilting, a triple metered ‘Presto’ brings the quartet to a festive end.

Lower strings kick off the swirling ‘Allegro’ that starts the D Minor Quartet, with the viola presenting the initial melody. Dense fugal passages populate this intricate 1st movement, which often finds the cello falling silent or using a sustained pedal note as the upper three voices assume dominance. A stately ‘Poco lento’ follows. Interweaving melodic lines feature paired voices, recombining in constantly shifting alignments as this relaxed middle movement develops. A vigorous unison phrase unites the brisk ‘Allegro con spirit’ that ends the work as a series of dissimilar episodes flash by.

Penned in E Flat, an easy ‘Allegro’ opens the final quartet, No.3 from the Op.3 set. An engaging dialogue between the first violin and viola is soon joined by the cello as a complex tapestry of superb counterpoint emerges. Gorgeously serene, the muted ‘Adagio’ in A Flat is one of the highlights of the disc. With alternating bittersweet passages in minor, this superb section ends all too soon. Resembling a joyous country dance, the triple metered ‘Poco presto’ carries the quartet and the CD to a bright and bubbly close.

Clear and detailed, the recording by CPO is up to its usual excellent standards. Sporting the name of one of the Classical era’s brightest lights, who now is barely recognized as a master of the string quartet, Pleyel Quartett Koln sparkles as it shines a spotlight on another forgotten composer. Led by the outstanding first violin of Ingeborg Scheerer, the German based group has unearthed these 5 excellent quartets by Wolf. They deserve to be heard.

Many people agree in that post-1985 Yellowman records are not worth a listen, that '85 marked the beginning of a steep decline for the toaster/Dj, but I deem a lot of his late 80s and early 90s output worthwhile, if in several different manners. This one from '88 is one of those.

With none other than Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare (Black Uhuru) in charge of the instruments and arrangements ( the most famous Jamaican rhythm section of all times) this album is dynamite, and if you can just sit in your couch while this plays, you're dead.

WAY more roots reggae than dancehall (although never loosing the toasting cadence of King Yellowman), the album takes you on a trip through very varied rhythms, incredibly intricate basslines, fantastic percussion and great arrangements, together with MESSAGE on the lyrics, a first in my experience. The guy is more focused now and the lyrics don't have the omnipresent sexual innuendo of past releases, but he still brags about how many women he's had around the globe. Priceless; gotta love him.

The sound is incredible but for somewhat lacking bottom end on 8 of the 10 tracks, but my beefy sub took care of that no problem. The recording is very even from one song to the other; there's practically no variation in tone and volume, which I loved. Very hi-fi.

Other albums you might like are ¨Yellow As Cheese¨ ¨Meets the Paragons¨ ¨Galong Galong Galong¨, ¨Prayer¨ and the more synth-sounding, pure electronic dancehall ¨Rambo¨

I've been a John Legend fan since I heard him on Kanye's debut album (before Ordinary People) so there's certain things I expect from the brother and he came through. The vocals were on point and the band hooked it up, especially on "Stereo".  He changed up the rhythm on a few of his old songs, which didn't take away from the songs at all.  If anything it enhanced them and made them more entertaining for a live setting.  So, that's the CD.  At first, the DVD felt like an afterthought to me but it got it's point across, "BUY THE LIVE DVD". There were a couple of music videos (love the one for "Show Me")and an interview he did for the concert, but the meat and potatoes of the DVD was the teaser for the actual concert DVD. From what I saw on the teaser it looks like I might have to pick that up as well. All in all, this makes a good addition to any CD collection. review_title: A terrific set of 20th Century, mainly German, art songs
review_text: Ernst Krenek is a 20th Century German composer who had a major hit with his opera 'Jonny Spielt Auf' in 1927.  And then he spent the rest of a long life wandering the world after the Nazis drove him from Germany, writing music furiously.  He never repeated the success of 'Jonny Spielt Auf' and the quality of his music seems to have been seriously uneven.  But there's a lot of it.  The wonderful soprano Christine Schaefer chose 21 songs from Krenek's huge output and thrills us with a beautiful voice and secure musicality.  This is modern stuff so the composer makes his singer work for her supper, but Schaefer takes it all in stride.  Krenek spent some time in the U.S. and some of the poems he set are in English.  There are even a few in French.  (Do I have to mention that this is part of the 'Musica Rediviva' series on Orfeo?  This is, like the 'Entartete Kunst' series on Decca, and attempt to bring music back that was suppressed by the Nazis.  Krenek was not Jewish, but he still had to run for his life.  I'm not sure that we have to envoke the Nazis to justify listening to this music.  It's terrific.  And good music gets forgotten-- and then rediscovered-- all the time, without help from the Nazis.)

Let me just start off by saying that this isn't for first time Hendrix auditors.
However, for those of us who have heard all of the offical releases, and still want more, this is good for that.
Disc one starts off with two songs originally issued on the album "In the West" which has long gone out of print, and its tracks gobbled up by both bootlegers and Jimi's own company. These songs are "Little Wing" and "Voodoo Child (Slight Return)" both are excellent. Then comes a high-energey version of "Purple Haze" from the second Albert Hall concert. It is followed briskly by Jimi's best recorded version of "Sunshine of Your Love" from the same concert. Then comes "Bleeding Heart" which is credited as featuring Jim Morrison, but he is inaudible on this track. This is probably the best track from that session, very blusey, not as good as the others, but not terrible. Then comes the infamous "Wake Up this Morning and Found Yourself Dead" also a jam, not terrible, but not Jimi's best. "Tomorrow Never Knows" is the next track, but here both Jimi and Jim are so stoned that this isn't quite a perfect preformance. We get a reprive from stoned songs with "Fire" a great version from the Albert Hall. Then is an edit of "Wild Thing" from the same concert. To end the disc is the bootleger's choice "Morrison Lament"- a terrible session with Jimi not really playing and Jim Morrison just screaming obcenities. Overall time: 49:03 Best track: "Voodoo Child (Slight Return)"
Disc 2 starts off with a widley cirulated version of "Red House",I am not quite sure from whence it comes but not Jimi's best rendition. "Good Times" is the next track, which as far as I can tell is either: a track with Lonnie Youngblood or Little Richard, OR a jam with the Band of Gypsys, the latter being most
likley, not bad! "Voices" and "Voice in the Wind" are presumably from the same session, not terrible, too much bass. "Voice in the Wind" is probably better. "Two and One Goes" is probably one of my favorite bootleg tracks, a good jam probably with "Gypsy Sun and Rainbows" but no one really knows. It's not even certain who wrote it. Then comes a rendition of the Rolling Stones' "Let Me Go"- which is really a quite good instrumental jam. "Uranus Rock" sees the return of Jim Morrison, this time Jimi acknowledges Jim's pointless wails. "Outside Woman Blues" is from the same session as the last song- one of the better ones from that set.
Then comes "Room Full of Mirrors" which is the full (extended) version from the second Albert hall concert, better than the original. Total disc time: 49:17 Best track: "Two and One Goes"
Disc 3 starts off with "Blues Blues" which sounds like a shorter version of "Wake Up This Morning and Found Yourself Dead". Then comes "Free Spirit" with Lonnie Youngblood, not terrible but not overly high quality. "Psycho" also featuring Youngblood is much like the previous track- mediocre. "Wipe the Sweat (2)" featurs an unfamiliar vocalist (Buddy Miles?) and a horn section - possibly something from Sky Church? Then comes "Groove Maker" from who-knows-where Little Richard? I don't think so. I'm not sure about this one.The next track, "Hot Trigger" is a really good song for a bootleg- really good. The next song "Nightlife" is another one of those mystery songs- not really good. The next song "You Got It" also has Youngblood- somewhere, not great. The next and last song with Lonnie Youngblood, "Suspicious" is good, the ones where Lonnie sings aren't bad at all, semi-funky. The next track "Goodbye Bessie Mae" I am almost certian is with Little Richard, it has to be. "She's A Fox" my all-time favorite Hendrix bootleg song. "Freedom and You" Little Richard again? I think just a demo jam. "She's So Fine"- oh, really? Probably a jam with some friends. "Sweet Thang" Sky Church? Overall disc time: 50:01 Best track: "She's A Fox"
Not bad, but not quite five stars, still good though, definatly worth a look!

"Yes, You" is not only one of the best CD's I've heard in a long while...it quickly vaulted to my desert island top 20! Jahn Xavier has had a long and interesting musical career...but if this 13-track CD is any indication...he's finally found the right recipe for music lovers who have been missing a certain type of "sound". It's hard to pigeonhole styles on this collection of tunes...but think about this : there's late 70s power pop, punky new wave chord structures, rockin' soul, R&B, old school torch songs...and all held together by the powerful, stylish and original voice of Jahn Xavier. Summing it up...It's the sounds of New York! It's hard to believe the Bowerytones are only two other guys (on bass and drums), who along with Jahn X. (who also plays guitar) create a larger sound. The production rocks, and I would expect to hear this on local NYC-area radio stations (WFUV, WFMU anyone?). My favorite tracks are (to me) a song cycle that begins with (4th song) "Bad Behavior" and flies right to and through "Under the Moon" (10th track). How many albums can you claim have 7 amazing tunes in a row? Not many I would say. "Yes, You" is so good...I want to hear more from Jahn Xavier and The Bowerytones...and soon!

review_title: That's the way it's got to be
review_text: After picking this up what hits you in the face is that life really aint fair. Here's a group that should've been everybit as huge as say the Searchers but were not even a blip on the US charts. They likely saw only minor chart action in their native UK. 2 stand out tracks are "Our love is fading away" & "Thats The way its got to be". The Poets had sublime harmony & to these ears every bit as good of the Searchers & also somewhat reminisent of their sound with the prominent 12 string guitar. But even with the help of Andrew Oldham they never found the kind of stardom they richly deserved. This group was not the same ol same ol crunching vox & loud bash & trash dance music but a more subdue & moody type folk sound with a distinct energy. If you like your 60s rock on the folky & harmonic side you will enjoy the Poets. Also, they wrote most of their own tunes & they are impressive. Only 4 stars due to somewhat trashy sound & I'm sure the engineer did the best he could but 2 songs have noticable hiss or deterioration (those may be some demos).

The Poets are indeed a strong contender for the title of Great Lost British Invasion group, and it is fitting that Amazon now carries this record. Despite signing with Rolling Stones manager Andrew Loog Oldham in 1964, and enjoying a minor British hit with their first single, major success was not to be. The Poets formed in Glasgow in 1963, and were quick to begin writing their own material. This was uncommon in 1963, and must have set them apart from the multitude of cover bands (even the Rolling Stones were essentially a cover band, albeit a great one, at this point.) Most of the time, the band favored a mournful, minor-keyed style not unlike a more guitar-based Zombies, (though this comparison only goes so far.) In addition, the Poets were distinguished by their usage of two twelve-string guitars, which provided them with a unique sound.

In analyzing the contents of Scotland's No. 1 Group, one must also be aware of another release entitled In Your Tower, another best of compilation for the Poets (not sold on Amazon). In the opinion of this writer, Scotland's No. 1 Group has the slight edge, even though there are a couple of good late 60's tracks on In Your Tower not on Scotland's No. 1 Group ("Dawn" and "Never Thought She Would"). Scotland's No. 1 Group has nine 1963-64 unreleased demos of original material not on In Your Tower, and they're of generally high quality. "With You By Me" would have made a fine catchy single in '63 or '64, while "Love Is Fading Away" was melodious folk-rock before the term really existed. "Miss Queen Bee" is a strong R&B raver unlike most of the band's other material, and makes one wonder why the band did not try this style more often. Despite the high quality of the songs, the demos occasionally suffer from some of the worst sound quality to ever grace a commercial release, but the patient listener can overlook such shortcomings. The remainder of the CD includes both sides of the six Decca single releases (fortunately of very good sound quality), and two excellent (if a bit raw) demo recordings from 1965. The Decca recordings are the high point of the Poets history, and represent some of the finest underappreciated British Invasion music. It is perplexing that the Poets never released a full-length album in the 60's. Based on the recorded evidence, they surely would have had enough material. In addition, after reading lead singer and main creative force George Gallacher's interview with Richie Unterberger (the full transcript is available on Unterberger's web site), it seems possible that even more unreleased Poets material exists in the Decca vaults.

Scotland's No. 1 Group is not the perfect anthology for the group, due to the aforementioned missing In Your Tower tracks, and other tracks rumored to exist in the vaults. However, as of 2006, Scotland's No. 1 Group is arguably the best overview available on the band. They deserve to be discovered. Indeed, for someone already into the Zombies and Searchers, the Poets are an excellent group to look into.

I still have the LP vinyl album. It has been played many times since my uncle John gave it to me. Unfortunately, I can no longer play it since I don't have a needle to play it on a record turntable. The album has suffered much since I played it as a teenager. It has a myriad of scratches and it skips quite a bit. But the music was incredible.

I am not a big fan of jazz, and my parents and other family never liked the music from this album. But I learned to appreciate jazz and even like jazz from this album.

I know very little of David Matthews, the composer but I liked this album. I just found a website that contains all the tracks of this album and played the entire album through from the internet. And it still sounds great.

The album is a combination of rock, jazz, with a touch of hip hop and even a bit of slow romantic swing, and a little classical.

Arrakis, the first piece on the album, represents the desert planet of the novel "Dune" which inspired the album. It is hauntingly beautiful as it starts off with an odd desolate sound, but then towards the middle of it, it takes on a jazzlike sound, like one stopped into a bar in an oasis in middle of this empty desert, and then toward the end it returns to the main theme of the desolation with a crecendo almost like an orgasm.

Sandworms is a different sound altogether. It has a very strong rock- jazz feel with heavy almost overpowering bass. I think it is the bass that makes this piece. It is unusual to find a piece of music that uses the bass as the main theme of a piece.

The Song of the Bene Gesserit is a soft, sweet, slow and enchantingly beautiful piece. It has a slow romantic feel -- like a slow jazz or swing dance piece or maybe slow rock. As I was listening to it again from the internet, I was imagining myself dancing with a young woman cheek to cheek, in a slow romantic dance.

Muad Dib is a fast piece which always makes me think of jumping and fighting Kangaroo rats. From the novel Dune, that was what the Muad Dib actually was and the hero of the story was nicknamed this, because of his resilience and ability to survive on the desert planet. This has a somewhat romantic feel too.

On the other side are David Matthews' versions of pieces from other writers. Which includes "A Space Oddity" by David Bowie, "Silent Running", and two themes from Star Wars, including Princess Leia's Theme, and the Main Title Theme.

I hope they republish this album for classic jazz and jazz-rock lovers and put it out on CD or something. I would buy it.

review_title: A treasure trove of late Brahms
review_text:
Here is more evidence that Brahms never quite wrote any mediocre music. Well, actually he did ... but it was his practice to trash pieces that did not meet his exacting standards. And such standards show their value in such marvelously conceived works as these late piano pieces. Not everyone knows that Brahms was a bonafied virtuoso at the piano and wrote a large ouevre of high-quality music that falls neaty into three periods: the early Beethoven-like 'heroic' style, the middle focus on the variation form and the introspective late works. Arthur Rubinstein said of Brahms' music: "It is with the late piano works, Op. 116-119, that we reach Brahms' most personal music for his chosen instrument. Brahms in his final years produced serene and nostalgic music that was ever more inward in mood ... and as his own notations in the score indicate, they are so intensely intimate that one cannot really convey their full substance to a large audience. They should be heard quietly, in a small room, for they are actually works for chamber music for the piano."

The late piano works are well recorded in the catalog (Lupu, Katchen, Cliburn, Gilels, Gieseking, Argerich, Perahia) and this Philips' DUO recording is among the better ones as a whole. Certainly the star of the three pianists featured here is Stephen Kovacevich - a firery yet tender-hearted pianist best known for his stellar Beethoven. Given his stature, it is a bit disappointing that the entire two-CD's were not all his playing as he recorded all the featured late works here. But, I suppose it is always good to give lesser-famous talent a chance to shine and make themselves better known.

One of these talents is Adam Haraseiwicz who turns in a crisp run at the Op. 35 "Paganini Variations" that has more of a cool, crisp precision than a red-hot flair to it - although a few pieces in the second book are especially impressive for their brilliant clarity. The theme was taken from Paganini's famous 24th Caprice in A-minor for solo violin. Kovacevich also performs the brilliant Op. 24 Variations equally admirably, evoking Handel's pomp-and-ceremony style with vigor. Both sets of variations are truly staturesque in the piano literature and reveal why Brahms was considered the greatest variationist since Beethoven.

The two Op. 79 Rhapsodies are dynamic concert showpieces with impassioned, chordal outer movements (marked "agitito" and "molto passioniato") surrounding an oasis of tender melody. No. 2 is one of Brahms' best-known piano works and a real crowd pleaser. These (along with the Op. 76 pieces) are given quite respectable readings by Dinorah Varsi, but their contrasting episodes of powerful virtuosity and tender lyricism are conveyed more effectively by the legendary Marth Argerich (Debut Recital, DG) or other pianists. But, the drama and mercurial brilliance in these pieces is so compelling that the pure music can override such aspects of performance.

But, the main event here are the four sets of Schumann-like piano "miniatures" performed by Stephen Kovacevich under various titles as Fantasies, Intermezzos, Ballades, Romance and Capriccios. In general they are of two moods: dramatic, romantic and virtuostic or slow, gentle and introspective. Some (like the E-flat Intermezzo Op. 117) reveal Brahms' equistite, tender-hearted talent for lullaby themes, where others (like the D-minor Capriccio Op. 116) harken to the dynamic flair of Scarlatti. All are masterful, and the gentle pieces are particularly beautiful. As in his Beethoven Sonatas, Kovacevich superbly expresses both sides of Brahms' moods. Most notably, his poetry and gentle expressivity in Op. 117 (three slow and lyrical pieces) and Op. 119 is among the finest recorded. And, as expected, he brings the needed "weight" to Brahms' most passionate utterences such as the powerfully chordal, Chabrier-like Rhapsody in E-flat, Op. 119.

Given such wonderous and consistent performances of Kovacevich here, it is disappointing that the sound quality is not as consistent. Both Op. 117 and Op. 119 (with the most beautiful slow movements) betray some unfortunate analog "hiss" that will be somewhat disturbing to expecially headphone listeners. In contrast, Op. 116 and 118 are much better, cleaner all-digital recordings. All others are "Digitalized by Bitstream" (Philips high-tech remastering technology) which must make some difference, but not enough in some spots. But, overall the sound is fairy bold and clear but with that typical circa-60's/70's inferior analog ambiance and extraneous "hiss." This is very typical of Philips' DUO sets by the way - they are usually "very good" but not the best in sound. But, I wouldn't let the sound stop you from getting this set.

Brahms' late music was a revelation to me for its inventiveness, quality and uncharacteristically intimate perspective. But, given that Brahms is one of the all-time masters of lyricism and sonority, this should be no surprise. While this set is inconsistent in both performers and sound quality, it still is a recommended set (also per Penguin Guide) - the least of the reasons being that is features all of Brahms' late piano music which is somewhat unique. If you are just starting to explore Brahms' piano music, the late works are the best place to start really. If you are looking ALL of Brahms' piano music, Julius Katchen's set is usually the most recommended but its sound is 60's vintage. Also, Radu Lupu's recordings are also a top choice for his equistite, poetic pianism that is most fitting to this music.

After purchasing the Naxos issue of the Galanta Dances, Marroszek Dances, and Peacock Variations I wanted to find recordings of these works in better sound. The Naxos is rather distant.

The Fischer seemed to be a logical choice, but it does not have the Peacock Variations. And that was what I wanted, not some little children singing folk songs as a filler. But, finding no other options in modern sound, I sprung for this one.

What a surprise. The children steal the show. They are the best part of this recording. The songs are ingratiating and the children's voices are superb. Philips should post haste make an entire CD of these choirs singing Hungarian folk songs.

The two dance suites are well played and are recorded with lots of detail that is missing in the Naxos. The Hary Janos is also well played and nicely recorded. But it will not replace the Dorati on Mercury, which is even better recorded and maxes out on the slapdash humor of this music. With Fischer this piece is very cute. With Dorati this piece is a downright hoot.

Even so, highly recommended.

"Invisible" is the second try of Edyta Gorniak in conquering of world market after modest international success of her outrageous self-titled English debut produced by Christopher Neil, who is responsible for success of Celine Dion.

This time most of songs were produced by team Absolute, which worked with Spice Girls or Tina Turner. The previous album was very nostalgic and even dance songs were very melancholic. "Invisible" is completely different. It's a happy album full of positive energy and contains a lot of songs in different types of dance music, including the biggest club hit from this set "Impossible", electronic "Can't Say No", 2step "Sit Down", up-tempo "Cross My Heart" or latin-flavored "As If" and "How Do You Know" and great r'n'b tune "Make It Happen". Of course Edyta didn't forget about emotional ballads, like another hits "The Story So Far", "Whatever It Takes" or haunting "Sleep With Me", which later was a hit for Conjure One.

This album is also very interesting because of quite intriguing production with many sound effects, which can be heard only on headphones. It's a great trump in such stylistical-varied material.

With such a voice and with such an album Edyta still has chances for being noticed all over the world.
