I love the opening scene showing the front of a house and a man sneaking around behind the curtains. A perfect scene for a horror film! When the game begins a big blue monster comes out of the door. Stab him with your sword. Avoid the bats and orange mice in the hallways. The object is to open doors and retrieve items in the gun cabinets, closets and other furniture sitting in each room.

In the outdoor section fight more bats and enjoy the fast music and green trees in the background. Watch out for big-mouthed catfish that jump out of the water. Prepare for blue blobs flopping around. The boss fight is some kind of crawlfish in a cave. Return the way you came avoiding the same enemies, and you know, the level music's really good!

In the main area with all the doors, climb the stairs, head into the left door and grab all the ammo you can in the cabinets and windows. When you do a scary-faced monster who looks like he ate too much pie appears! Stab him because that's what you do with pie eater faces.

Enter a cave section and avoid floating blue gargoyles, bouncing blobs, jerky overlarge skeletons and bats. You can shoot fireballs so I recommend doing so at the skeletons and gargoyles. The boss fight is a floating fireball spitting ghost. He's actually pretty scary. Write down the password after the fight and leave this area.

In the main hallway open more windows and cabinets for items. In the next cave area battle more blobs, bats, gargoyles, shaky skeletons and skeleton heads. The boss fight is an orange sheep dog that runs back and forth across the floor. Use the ladder in the middle to climb down and shoot at him when he reaches the left or right side, then leave. Be careful because the amount of gargoyles roaming around just got real.

In the main area with the doors, fight another blue monster. Monsters like to make sneak appearance in the main area after you finish collecting items from the furniture. Perhaps it's because you're breaking into their rooms and stealing their stuff. In the water section you're in the water with the big mouthed fish! They swim frantically just to keep you on your toes. The level design is very bland by the way. So far I'm not impressed with the levels. You don't actually swim either- just walk slowly in the water.

The boss fight is a sea turtle with a blue shell. Stab him in the eye. Since he takes a long time to swim to you, you'll have lots of time. There's a second phase to this fight. Mini turtles scamper around the room. Leave this area. Yes that's right- leave through this looooong water area with repetitive fish. The fact they'd make you backtrack through all this goes to show what kind of bland game this is.

In the next cave area avoid swirling skeleton heads, forming bats, blobs, disco jerky skeletons, gargoyles and a tiny patch of water with one jumping big mouthed fish. The boss fight is a blue mummy that shoots blue balls at you. You must climb down the ladder and shoot him with fireballs while he's stationary. If you're lucky you'll get in one or two shots per attempt.

In the next stage... well it's more water. At least the setting is nice with the green trees in the background. Take on swarms of fish, bats, gargoyles, etc. This level's short. The boss fight is a big mouthed plant/worm hybrid that shoots miniature shrimp at you.

Time for another area, and you know there's really not a lot of diversity going on here at all. More green trees, more bats, blobs, floating skeleton heads, yet another cave area, more ladder climbing, etc. A boss fight with a scary gargoyle who shoots fireballs at you. The way he flies around is pretty scary I have to admit. Reminds me of an old McDonald's commercial where people float around. Like aways write down the password and leave.

In the next forest/cave area, you know, same ol' enemies. The boss fight is a rolling bowling ball gargoyle creature. You're given a space in the middle to jump over him as he rolls by. Shoot at him as he rolls back and forth. Bland fight. When you return to the main area with all the doors you can access the basement area with more mice and bats. Another forest/water with the same enemies. Wait no, a different enemy! Rocks that bounce up and down tossing mini chunks of ice at you. The boss fight is a Castlevania snake detached from the side of the wall so he bounces around the room.

The boss fight in the next vine area is a skull head with several bones spinning around his head as he floats around the room. When the bones come together he forms a floating rock. Weird! I know it's a little late to be mentioning this, but the music that plays while exploring the rooms for items is really bland and reminds me of a certain jungle theme in Yoshi's Island DS. The music in that game was criticized pretty bad, so I imagine if more people were familiar with Dr. Chaos, it would have been criticized just as often.

You'd think the final area would be filled with better enemies and a different area like most games when you get close to the end. Instead it's the same shaky skeletons, jumping fish, bats, gargoyles and skull heads we've seen before (granted, the harder ice shooting blue skull heads). Same ol' vine area too. The final boss fight is a fireball spitting male lion sitting high on a platform. Shoot at him from the platform on the other side and he'll go down soon enough. And that's it! There's no story so we can only guess what's going on when we see the ending showing a young boy walking up to a grown man. Perhaps it's his father and the two are reunited.

Overall an okay game, but repetitive levels and enemies really hamper this game so it has no replay value for me. Maybe others will really like it though. It's an okay action game at least. I do enjoy the level and ending music at least. The enemies are nicely animated too.

The Guardian Legend is a fascinating game blending Gradius-style jet fighter shooting with Zelda-like exploration. These two *very* different styles coming together is quite the treat, and the music? *Extremely* good. Arguably better than Gradius or Zelda. I personally enjoy it more than 80% of the NES library, and I think VERY highly of NES music overall!

You're immediately thrown into a Gradius style stage as the game begins. Should be noted that all jet fighter portions of the game involve the screen auto scrolling upwards, whereas in Gradius you constantly go to the right. The boss fight is a series of traps that toss dynamite your way. Shoot 'em all! You soon find out through text that you must destroy 10 safety devices so a self-destruct sequence will be activated, and the world will be saved.

You then morph into the Zelda style overworld. The music is so good here I can't stand it! The gameplay is even like the original Legend of Zelda where every screen provides a different set of obstacles. You battle purple spiders, blue blobs that come out of the ground, crabs, and another boss fight- this one being some kind of orange monster that pops out of the ground. You're trapped here until he's defeated.

More crabs, spiders, marble-resembling creatures, fire bats, a jellyfish boss (again you're trapped until he's defeated), bouncing orange rocks and more. Now you're back to the Gradius-style gameplay with a beautiful dark blue setting of pine trees below as you battle yellow fish, dynamite flinging enemies, seahorses, eyeball aliens, a unique ground-destroying eyeball enemy and stingrays. This time the boss fight is a fireball-spitting skeletal piranha. I don't know what it is, but the victory music is SO cool! The way the final three notes extend at the end... ah, nobody probably understands what I mean because I can't explain myself man!

Back to the overhead Zelda style action. The setting is now dark blue as you arrive to a different corridor. That is the theme of this game by the way- as far as the Zelda portions go, travelling and warping from one corridor to another. The same spiders, bouncing orange and purple rocks and hermit crabs are waiting for you here. The boss fight is a green crab... you know I should be calling these mini bosses because the bosses you face in the jet fighter areas are much longer and more elaborate, not to mention bigger in appearance. More fire bats, marbles, and electrical spiders? Yup! Watch out they can expand into numerous spiders if you stick around long enough! A purple jellyfish boss afterwards. The game's slowly getting harder because this enemy is more persistent than the previous bosses.

More shooting action in your jet fighter. This time a swamp or beach setting battling starfish, dynamite shooting creatures, orange fish, stingrays, alien eyeballs... more or less the same enemies you fought in the previous stage, and the boss fight is some kind of one-eyed laser beam shooting sea urchin. Back to the Zelda style gameplay with marbles, fire bat, spiders and a carrot-shaped blob enemy who spits numerous laser balls. You know the little orange things that come out of the ground resemble what I used to call hershey kisses in the Zelda dungeons! The blue crab boss shoots laser balls like mad, and later the purple jellyfish is a little angrier than last time too.

More shooting stages. This time the fish are gray, the stingrays are still persistent, the action moves faster, the setting remains dreary with the pine trees below and the piranha boss has turned angry. You're back on land shortly, just to proceed with the next shooting stage. This time the action is pretty intense! The fishes have turned red, the dynamite enemies are numerous, the seahorses are back, the eyeball aliens are more plentiful, and now there's snakes on top of the screen. I don't even know what the blue-shelled creatures are but they're scary. The starfish are numerous and the boss fight is a lobster.

Back on land you're warping from one corridor to another until you find the forest stage with the same spiders, jumping orange rocks and marble enemies you fought in the other areas. But the boss fight is a spinning green wheel that chases you around. Enemies are snails or scorpions after this, carrot-shaped blobs and ah, good memories! The very first boss of the game that pops out of the ground. He's back and just as easy as ever.

Oh hey, since you're in a forest area this means the jet fighter stages have changed into forest areas as well. The trees below create a nice scenery as you battle fireball-spitting plants (and they spit a LOT), yellow dragons, more tree varieties and the boss fight is some kind of disappearing/reappearing mechanical thing that shoots missiles in a circle. Pretty dangerous. Time for another shooting stage. This one has mushrooms, swinging aliens that look like deranged mushrooms, more plants that shoot fireballs than most people can probably handle (definitely more than I can handle!) and the boss fight is the sea urchin returning but MUCH harder this time. Wow I can't figure out the pattern at all to his laser beams so luck is required to defeat him.

You now return to the same area you were in, in the beginning of the game (with that super catchy music) and for the most part the enemies haven't changed... except for these menacing red and blue alien creatures found in one room. They're pretty scary and unexpected! Back to the forest stage with more spiders, scorpion snails, fire bats, bouncing orange rocks, orange hershey kisses, and the boss fight is a purple jellyfish. Soon a spinning purple wheel chases you around the room- not a hard boss but kind of annoying.

Another shooting stage. Laser beam shooting lobsters, fire bats that fly from a protective cave below, spikes launching from plants, swaying mushroom-like aliens and the boss is another mechanical thing with legs that open and close, and upon destroying the legs the body remains and chases you around. This reminds me of something from War of the Worlds and it's quite creepy! Another shooting stage... and oh my, the screen moves WAY too fast here. All the laser beam shooting lobsters, fireball spitting plants, red dragons, swaying aliens, mushrooms and spikes don't help either (and if all THAT isn't enough- there's plenty of debris that will probably do the bulk of the hitting). The boss fight is a disappearing/reappearing fireball spitting dragon.

Back to the Zelda-ish portion you're now in some kind of underground futuristic area, and it doesn't take long to face your first boss. It's a bunch of spiders that come out of the ground. Not much of a threat. You then see glowing floating colorful tile enemies, jumping rocks (not just orange and green ones either), spiders, blue hershey kisses, scorpions and a crab boss. Oh wow! The shooting stage is futuristic as well. Expect to see red dragons, enemies made of swirling fireballs, blue shells, starfish and the boss fight is another sea urchin with laser beam shooting abilities. I gotta say, all this action in the shooting stages is hard to keep up with. I don't necessarily hate it- it's fun on some level, but I don't feel like I can master every enemy movement when you have to dodge so many things.

Back on land you face more spiders, crabs and fire bats. The boss fight is a blue jellyfish. Gee haven't seen that one before (yeah yeah, sarcasm). You soon battle a giant snowflake. Pretty strange, and maybe it's just me but the regular spider enemies are getting bigger soon after. More scorpion snails, electrical expanding spiders and colorful tiles. The following shooting stage with its gray background reminds me of a drawing. I find it really unique. You battle homing blue shells, fire pigeons, yellow dragons, green starfish, shard spitting purple volcanoes and a bouncing fireball spitting lobster boss.

You're back on land but it's brief. Back to the skies! Oh wow the purple background is really cool. Some tricky moving spikes, laserball spitting spiders, blue homing shells... and a return of the mechanical boss with legs! Blast the legs, but watch out for the giant fireballs after the separation. This boss means business. Back on land the same marble enemies (seriously they're not marbles but what *are* they exactly!), fire bats, bouncing rocks, spiders... yup. Another shooting stage, this one completely dominated by shard spitting volcanoes and spikes. The boss fight is a small hand glider. Ha! After all the bigger more impressive bosses, it's almost comical to see something like this.

We've now entered what looks like the inside of an aliens body with the pink walls all around. Neat! A bubble spitting crab boss is next. Enemies include green worms, marbles, red aliens (the scary ones I mention above), carrot shaped blobs, blue bats and more. The shooting stage consists of those giant blue creatures that scare me, tiny green spider aliens, floating eyeballs, mushroom-resembling swaying aliens, shiny blue octopus mushrooms, wiggling green snakes... and I love the music here by the way. The boss fight reminds me of the thing from Link to the Past- dungeon 6 (Vitreous is his name). It's a 4-eyeballed boss but not too hard.

Back in the weird pink walled world you battle more red aliens and marbles. Shooting stage number... who knows by this point. Probably 20. At least they're getting prettier. Just look at that purple/red background! Enemies include floating octopus mushrooms, swaying aliens, laser beam shooting spiders, floating eyeballs, green alien spiders, gigantic bubble spitting blue shells... and the boss fight is the same 4-eyeballed thing from the previous stage, however there's now swaying aliens and wiggling snakes interfering with the action.

Back on land carrot shaped blobs, blue bats, bouncing rocks and the spider boss returns (you know, the boss that pops out of the ground and spreads into 4 spiders). Now you'll see crabs, scorpion snails and another spinning wheel boss. More black marbles, blue bats, spiders, more jellyfish... the jellyfish are now regular enemies! That's how you know the challenge is going up (and it's BEEN going up all along, now it's definitely getting intense!) What the? There's guards running down the screen! Another shooting stage with stingrays, octopus mushrooms, twirling rock-shaped enemies that break apart and throw their fireball remains at you. Now it's time for the longest boss fight in the game- a floating alien head covered in eyes. He turns bronze and gets more fireball happy in the second phase. This is hard stuff! Can you make it?

Another shooting stage. Floating green alien spiders, enemies shaped like fireballs that launch at you, floating eyeballs, octopus mushrooms, stingrays.. and *groans!* The boss fight is a return of the floating alien head! And it's JUST as long of a battle. He floats back and forth shooting laser balls, and it takes forever to complete. You now find yourself in the final area- the desert. Green spiders, marbles, jumping colorful rocks, soldiers marching down the screen, jellyfish, a FAST moving red crab boss, and another one of those spider bosses come up from the ground afterwards.

A shooting stage in the desert. Prepare to battle skull heads, laser balls, laser beam shooting spiders, bouncing statues, twirling rocks, big dynamite spitting skulls. The boss fight is some kind of square-shaped red moth. It's boring looking. Back on land you battle more colorful jumping rocks, red hershey kisses and statue enemies. Another shooting stage. Dynamite spitting skull heads, statues that open up and release smaller skull head, laser beam shooting spiders, rocks that turn blue and come at you, laser balls, blue shells, laser beam shooting statues that bounce around, enemies that twirl around and throw rocks and a boss fight with a menacing looking laser beam shooting skull head. This is too much!

Back on land to battle more swift moving guards, red hershey kisses, blue jellyfish, bouncing rocks, marbles and green spiders. In the second phase of the desert (with different music) you battle a fireball spitting giant skull head as a boss. Afterwards green spiders, bouncing green rocks, carrot shaped blobs, soldiers, worms, blue bats and red hershey kisses. I LOVE the music here- sounds relaxed but tension-building as well. It's caught somewhere in between which makes me nervous. HA! The hand glider from an earlier shooting stage is now a mini boss in the Zelda portion of the gameplay!

Another shooting stage. This one has skull launching statues, red shards, blue shards, laser beam shooting statues, twirling enemies that toss rocks at you, a return of those eyeball ground-destroying enemies from earlier in the game and dynamite spitting dragon skulls (except they spit skulls this time!) The menacing laser beam shooting skull head returns. Back on land red and blue jellyfish, red hershey kisses, green spiders, worms and carrot shaped blobs.

You guessed it- another shooting stage. Laser beam shooting spiders, laser beam shooting bouncing statues, ground opening eyeball enemies, floating blue shards, rocks coming alive and going after you and big bull skulls (I like how they're attached to a snake skeleton before launching at you). The boss fight is a third meeting with the legged machine. Simply destroy the legs then take care of the body.

The final shooting stage in the game. It takes place in the desert like the last 5-6 have. The music's a little strange here. The first enemy you encounter is that floating one-eyed piranha skull from earlier in the game, then the bouncing lobster boss from earlier, the machine with legs (which is really overkill by this point), the sea urchin (overkill as well), the floating alien with eyes (once again it takes too long, ugh) and the boring disappearing/reappearing machine boss I mention above that resembles a moth. Nice boss gauntlet, but the second phase takes place in outerspace where you battle a blue alien with claws that reach down to grab you. He turns orange and red the more damage he takes, but watch out for those missiles!

Overall Guardian Legend is a great game and it *is* underrated, but let's be honest, quite a bit of the game is similar to a game I positively can't stand (the Adventures of Dino Riki) in the overbearing amount of enemies that appear on screen. That's a problem, but at least Guardian Legend feels more fair (make that a LOT more fair). Trying to beat this game is going to be a huge challenge as a result. You can spend chips and pick up hearts to restore your life which helps. Otherwise I enjoy the fast-paced gameplay. The story portions are usually short and sweet which I like. It probably would've been hard to pay attention to a story after my nerves are still shaking from all the shooting stages anyway, lol. Still a great game, but not quite a classic.

review_title: oh please, this game is horrible!
review_text:
Super Black Bass might have better graphics and sound than the original Black Bass on the NES, but that doesn't mean *anything* to me!

One big problem: where are all the fish??? I throw my line in the water and, even though the water LOOKS better on the Super NES than on the NES, the waves can actually make me seasick (and I found out last year what it's like to be seasick, and it's really a bad feeling!)

I don't get it: I sit there with my line in the water. 20 minutes go by and I STILL haven't seen a fish! It's like in real-life when you fish in the Atlantic Ocean after a hurricane (or any kind of severe storm) and all of a sudden NOTHING is there. Where did all the fish go? Playing the Black Bass on the NES was a lot more fun because you had fish coming out the you-know-what. In the NES game, lots and lots of fish came up and took the bait, in a matter of minutes. In this version, 20 minutes go by and I STILL don't see anything!

When I finally DO see a fish (after taking a nap) it never gets near my line, so I'm left feeling like I wasted all that time.

Super Black Bass gives you more options than the NES version, but it doesn't matter since you can never catch any fish. This game didn't go down as a classic *thankfully* (which I was concerned might happen 8 years ago). Skip it! Pick up the original NES Black Bass instead and have a fishingly good time! If you pick up this version, pack a few extra sandwiches!

Rogue Legacy is devilishly delicious and wickedly funny. Combining a dose of nostalgia with a dab of amusing nuances and addictive gameplay, Rogue Legacy for all three PlayStation platforms takes what was best about the PC version and ups it repeatedly for a truly definitive.

Rogue Legacy released for the PC and OnLive users on June of 2013, which was followed by a Macintosh and Linux version the next October. The title received well across all of the aforementioned platforms, being praised for its difficulty, “broader progression system,” and unique stylings. Recently, Rogue Legacy made the jump to consoles and has been refined to fit consoles a little bit better. All of the updates that slowly hit the original incarnations of the game have been bundled together along with some balance and difficulty tweaks.

Essentially the game places the player as an ambiguous knight (usually with a hilarious name) and the character is tasked with exploring an ever-shifting castle. As the game progresses the character battles numerous types of monsters while collecting coins, blueprints, runes, and other long lost artifacts. Initially the castle is available, but as more of the map is uncovered and (more-importantly) as the knight levels up and progress other more difficult areas open up. Each of these pre-defined areas, which are procedurally generated between deaths, have a boss.

Once the boss is defeated…the boss remains defeated. The game promotes repetition and leveling to defeat the bosses. Hardcore, skilled gamers will find much challenge in this setup, while those who enjoy the difficulty, but may not have a lot of time to play, will also enjoy the quick-pacing and eventual level progression that’ll make the bosses all that much more easier— Time over a ridiculous learning curve.

The real nuts and bolts of Rogue Legacy stem from death. As the player dies, instead of respawning, the character chooses an heir to carry on the family quest. The heir is chosen by making a selection from a group of three randomly generated characters. These characters oftentimes have weird and unusual abilities that’ll effect the style of gameplay, the character’s attack, health, and combat/magic abilities, as well as the general feel of the character.

The player also retains his or her gold from the prior play session and can then use it to purchase upgrades to the family manor, which ultimately upgrades all subsequent characters. From the manor screen, there is another section which allows the user to strike up a conversation with a myriad of sellers which provide weapons, armor, and magical armaments. There is even an architect, which can be paid a percentage to prevent the castle from randomly changing, so if a particular room is giving you trouble and you die you can pay to have the castle remain the same (instead of being procedurally generated) and tackle it once more (this can be done ad infinitum).

Rogue Legacy harkens back to an older era of gaming. The art style is pixelated and colorful and the music is reminiscent of the more-limited chipsets of yesteryear. Akin to such games as 1001 Spikes and Dark Souls in difficulty, Rogue Legacy will give most players a run for their money, however, the slick progression system, rich sense of humor, and overall cadence of the game is perfect for hardcore gamers or those wanting to play in bits on a commute or with only a couple minutes of downtime. Plus, Rogue Legacy is cross-buy and cross-save on all three PlayStation platforms, so with a challenging experience, cohesive gameplay, and a great aesthetic there is a lot to be had by Cellar Door Games’ Rogue Legacy.

The carrying bag is great! Not only can you use it to carry your Wii Balance Board, but I use it even more as a storage bag for my small equipment: bands, controllers, weights, and other miscellaneous equipment.

The ankle and wrist weights are comfortable and add resistance for a more strenuous workout. The weights included in this set are a bit lighter than another set that I own, so I recommend them for someone who is just starting to add weights.

The armband is handy, but I had trouble finding a Wii program in which I could use it. Perhaps it's used more for games. I don't play many games. Most of my programs require holding the Wii in my hand. Also, be aware that the Wiimote will only fit in the armband as is. If you put the Wiimote in a case, it will not fit.

The leg holster is perfect! I have two other ones and both of them slip down my leg. This one doesn't! The best I've found so far - love it!

A good pedometer can cost as much as this entire kit, so I wasn't surprised to learn that the pedometer is not a big selling point. It's cheaply made. I recommend buying a good one made by Omron.

I love the stepper! This one folds up fairly compact, making it easy to store and carry. It fits well on the Wii Balance Board. The board and stepper are very stable once you have them in place. There's no need to worry that the board will rock off the stepper. The only issue I have with the stepper is with weighing in. When it's on carpet, it's not very accurate. My husband cut a board to put between it and carpet, which helps; but if I really want an accurate weight, I have to take the Balance Board off the stepper and weigh on the Balance Board alone. Other than that, I love the stepper. The extra effort required to use the stepper with the Wii provides a much better aerobic exercise. I use this with almost all of my Wii exercise programs including Wii Fit Plus, EA Sports Active, and EA Active 2.

The exercise mat is a nice addition if you don't have one already. It lies flat, it's comfortable, and it's pretty!

Finally, there's a lanyard. Again, this is a fun addition, but not really the reason I'd buy the kit. For me, the stepper, carrying bag, weights, and leg holster are more than enough reason to buy the kit.

review_title: A good port of some good NES games
review_text:
The port/emulation of these five games is excellent. Both sound and graphics seem to be basically identical to the originals running on the NES. These games really need a decent control pad to be fully enjoyed. With one, the control is equivalent to the originals. Konami did a great job with the game's front end, in that once the application is launched, all functions can be accessed solely by a game pad (including switching games, changing settings, etc.). It's also possible to save a game's state at any time, which is the only upgrade over the original games.

All 5 games are actually surprisingly playable, considering their age, but some more so than others. The two Contra games I could do without, although I've spent an hour or two on them (I still find them way to difficult). The first Castlevania isn't much of anything special either. Castlevania 2 was the first game in the series to add some Adventure/RPG elements, and is the main reason I bought this compilation. It's nowhere near as good as Symphony of the Night or the GameBoy Advance Castlevania games, but I'm enjoying it.

Castlevania 3's gameplay moves closer to the original's, except with considerably enhanced graphics and music (for a NES game that is). Most notably it added multiple paths through the game-at the end of many levels the player is given two paths to pick from. It also added three potential alternate characters with different abilities. The combination of those two elements gave Castlevania 3 quite a bit of replay value back in the day (although I only actually beat the game once-it gets extraordinarily hard towards the end).

My only "complaint" is just that I'd love to see more compilations like this. The NES and other systems from that era have a huge backlog of games with gameplay that still holds up today, and I'd love the opportunity to buy more of them! At any rate, if you don't mind the dated graphics, this compilation is a good deal, especially for the price.

review_title: An early attempt at survival horror
review_text:
Considering the hardware restraints and censorship issues of the NES, it was very difficult to make a game approaching anything resembling scary. Taking everything into consideration, Dr. Chaos on the NES came as close to a genuine effort at a survival horror game as can be expected. True, it would be hard to convey horror on an 8 bit system even if censorsip wasn't an issue, but as it is, Dr. Chaos has several things going for it. The setting is familiar, as are the enemies (a decrepit mansion filled with rats and monsters) and the action is presented from a side view. However, enter a door and things get interesting. The view switches to first-person, and the player moves a cursor around the room to explore with commands: "get," "go," open," and "hit," to aquire items and weapons. The player can use a compass to tell which direction they are facing, and can move from room to room. The trick is, though, because the good Doctor's experiments have rearranged the mansion, the layout of these rooms is different EVERY TIME. The game can be saved via password, but the experience is completely random. Further complicating things, the player must navigate these rooms to find secret passages to the boss monsters, and the key items they hold. Worse still, when a door or cabinet is opened, there is a chance a monster will pop out and chase the player out of the room and into the side-scrolling corridor, where they must be beaten. If you aren't prepared for it, (and you rarely are, as there is no warning) this can be startling.

Its true the graphics aren't especially strong, and the action can be standard fare. Where the game shines is in the exploration part, where you never know what to expect, and the atmosphere is more tense. The music does a decent job of conveying the urgency and tension of most of the scenes, and particularly noteworthy are the main theme and boss themes. In fact, the intro screen is one of the best parts of the game---watch it and see.

Much has been said of the poor design of the monsters in the game. It is average, and even though better is out there, it could be a lot worse. The fighting mechanics of the game are solid; no particular nuances or difficulties can be found, though your protagonist does tend to be a bit on the faint-hearted side.

Dr. Chaos is a large game, and fans of adventure games will find a long oddysey ahead of them, as well as more than a few surprises. Because of the unique nature of the two scenes---the side-scrolling adventure and the exploration scenes---it is an NES game with a unique flavor, made more so because of the horror motif. Resident Evil it isn't, but anyone looking for Resident Evil on the NES should be directed to Capcom's "Sweet Home," a game that came later and was never released in the states anyway. For everyone else, Dr. Chaos is a great bargain and a unique title for the NES.

THE GOOD: Room exploration is tense and different every time, varied game scenes break up monotony, music ranges from good to very good, much longer than average NES game, saved via password, horror theme is maintained throughout

THE BAD: monster design could be better, graphics could be better, randomization of exploration makes it difficult to strategize, main character is somewhat weak

review_title: Glad I stumbled upon this one
review_text:
As a big fan of real-time strategy games, I feel lucky to have stumbled across this one. I haven't played any of the earlier Warlords Battlecry games, so I didn't really know what to expect. However, this one (WBC3) turned out to be a real gem. Yes, it's dated in both gameplay and look, but to get stuck on its appearances is to miss the larger point about all of the things that the game gets right.

Gameplay: It's a somewhat traditional RTS game, with resource collecting, base-building, and map exploration. However, even these aspects are handled in a fun way. Resource-collecting is not done via the back-and-forth trips of peons, but instead resources are "captured" by meditating hero and general units (more of these shortly). Base-building is structured around five tiers, which unlock various units and abilities. The most interesting dynamic in the whole game is the roleplaying elements. Nearly every unit can level up and become stronger, and each side has a hero unit. These units are created before a match and are persistent. You can name them, determine their class, race, and even appearance (in a limited way). There are a whopping 16 races in the game and at least as many classes, ranging from paladin and archmage to deathknight and necromancer. The races are fairly distinct, with very little overlap in units or buildings. As you level up in your chosen class (done by killing enemies and winning battles), you will unlock and enhance various abilities and stats. It's really a well-done, fun part of the game that gives it more longevity than the typical RTS game. Some maps have little quests that you can perform for rewards, and your hero can acquire various items (weapons, armor, magical loot, etc.) by killing other heroes, neutral bosses, or completing missions. You can get quite attached to your hero over time (and you can create as many as you'd like, but can only use 1 per match). You can also earn a retinue that includes generals who can fight with you from battle to battle, until they are killed (there's even a graveyard screen for you to remember deceased members of your retinue!). It's just a really well thought out and creative system that keeps the game from being just another RTS game.

There is a single-player campaign that allows you to create a hero and adventure with him/her across the lands of Etheria in search of the "fifth horseman." It's rather standard fare for these kinds of games and is really about teaching you how to play the game. Nothing particularly exciting, and it would be a bit bland if not for the hero dynamic and the ability to play various races in the campaign. The skirmish mode is quite fun and well constructed, and the skirmish AI is pretty good and adjustable. You can play with various win conditions, create random maps, set up teams, determine difficulty level of AI players, and so forth. There is even a map editor. Overall, there are a lot of custom options in skirmish mode that should suit the taste of many players, including Ironman mode which results in the permanent death of your hero if s/he gets killed in a match.

The problems with WBC3 are relatively minor, but all together they keep me from giving the game 5 starts. I would have liked to have been able to set up team matches using any one of the win conditions (such as Fortress), but some of the win conditions are limited to free-for-all matches or online multiplayer. You also cannot set starting positions on random maps nor is there a camera-zoom feature. Base-building is expected in RTS games, but this game has a few too many buildings that need to be constructed in order to unlock various units and abilities. Thus, you cannot really avoid the ugly base sprawl that plagued the last generation of RTS games. Beyond having a map editor, this game really should have come with modding tools that allowed for further customization and creativity. There are some tools scattered across the internet if you don't mind looking for them, but they really only allow for the tweaking of hero and unit stats, along with a few other things. Individually, these issues will not keep most people from enjoying this game; however, they may limit the replayability a bit.

Graphics: Dated to be sure, but still quite serviceable. Actually, the game (at 1280x1024 resolution) looks better than I was expecting, though it does not match the looks of contemporaries like Dawn of War or Battle for Middle Earth. The maps are well detailed, and the buildings and unit animations are convincing enough. Just don't expect this game to measure up to some of the better-looking RTS games out there.

Sounds: Most things are fine in the audio department. Most units have verbal (or at least audible) acknowledgments. Sound effects are appropriate; I believe that you can even shift between a male or female narrator. Some of the voice acting is quite good, and a few of the units have humorous lines. The music gets a bit repetitive over time, but no big deal.

Technical issues: The game has been quite stable on my computer, at least with the 1.03.24 patch (I purchased the game at [...] for $9.99 already patched). I also still run on XP SP3--I'm just old school like that!). A helpful .pdf manual comes with it, and hero and spell manuals can be found on the internet. If you decide to mod the game, be sure to backup the original files. Also, there is no annoying DRM of any kind in the game (at least not the GOG version).

Replayability/Value: I was hooked on this game for a solid 3 weeks, playing skirmishes, modding, and finishing the campaign. I still haven't played with about half of the 16 races or most of the different hero classes. Thus, the replay value is quite high. There are a few major mods on the internet, but I haven't used any of them. Much of the game is hard coded, so I don't think that really deep modding is possible without some skill and commitment. Since you can buy this game for as little as $10, it's a very good value. I don't suppose that there is much of a multiplayer base out there now for online matches, but the single-player content is robust enough to warrant a purchase. I highly recommend the game to any RTS gamer or even those who like roleplaying games with a twist.

Pros:
+Huge number of races, classes, units, maps, and customization options
+Hero and roleplaying systems
+Loot drops and mini-quests, even in skirmish mode
+Skirmish options
+Random map generator
+Skirmish AI can pose a good challenge
+Campaign is decent
+Technically stable
+No DRM!

Cons:
-Limited modding possibilities with available tools
-Too many buildings and inevitable base sprawl
-No camera-zoom option
-Limited number of win conditions for team matches

This cable does work and produces acceptable RGBS. I'm using it with the SPECIALTY-AV SCART to Component Converter to connect to a Trinitron CRT.

The problems in this cable are related to poor quality build and design. The DC connector is not particularly high quality and even slight movement results in some image issues. Just make sure that you seat the connector carefully. Furthermore, the SCART end is not engineered correctly. While most of the design is OK and follows proper spec, the resistor on pin 15 is only 75 Ohm, resulting in an output voltage that would be approximately 6V DC (halved from the DC's 12V DC output) which is twice what should be provided to be within the 3V DC spec for a SCART input. So there is a slim but unlikely chance that this cable could damage a display. In my case, the attached YPbPr converter probably doesn't use pin 16 but it's still worth noting.

General build quality of the SCART head is on-par with what I'd expect from a cheap cable from China. Essentially hot glue and some capacitors wired right into the RGB pins. Some were nearly making contact with one another. No nice quality PCB. If you want quality, look elsewhere. This cable is also not shielded.

review_title: Quality materials and easy assembly; could use some refinement
review_text:
My son-in-law is an avid gamer and needed a vertical stand/holder for his PS5 system. This Musvoh vertical wall hanging mount looked very promising so I got it for him. Here's what he had to say about it after assembling it and fitting his PS5 into it.

He notes: "I'd rate it a 4 out of 5 stars. It had all of the necessary hardware, but I don't trust the drywall anchors (see photos) it came with to support the weight of it all (PS5 systems weigh about 14 lbs). Assembly itself was straightforward. The sheet metal parts (anodized aluminum and stainless steel) are very sturdy and well manufactured. The anodized surface looks nice, but the metal plates that support the ps5 are flat, whereas the ps5 is contoured, so there are gaps which detracts from the appearance. I also feel that they could have designed it such that the outer lip (at the front of the platform) doesn't protrude so much. I plan to use better drywall anchors (and try to screw into a wall stud) and to mount it behind the TV so it will be out of sight--I think it's good for that application. If you want to mount your PS5 somewhere visible, I'd suggest getting a different mounting system."

The setup was very easy to do with the instructions that came with. I love that it's wireless. Solid build and very durable. The keys are also very quiet they don't have a loud clacking sound. I would recommend this.

review_text:
This game rocks. You will never find a better fighting/adventure game anywhere. The graphics are perfect, the controls are awesome and the story is cool. I've never had this much fun playing a super-hero game. I could play this game and beat it a million times and it would still be just as fun. review_title: Definitely an improvement.  A few requests though...
review_text:
I definitely am enjoying this one more than the first. Improved handling physics. I am really enjoying the Irish courses this time around.

For the Developers - some things that would really make it more enjoyable:

First, let us practice races within Career mode. It is a pain to have to keep jumping out of career mode to get to know the track before we make the commitment to actually race within Career mode. This is a hard game and without knowing the tracks well you really don't have a chance. Also, in Ireland, you need to highlight the actual race course on the mini-map as there are lots of intersections that you don't know which way to go - until you're right on top of it.

Second, PLEASE improve REPLAY mode. These courses are beautiful but you don't really get to enjoy them while you're racing and the replay mode isn't very good at all. You could drop butt view altogether (does anyone really enjoy that view?). Add off track views for the entire replay - as if there is one camera after another along the track to give continuous spectator views. Check out the RIDE games...they have nailed REPLAY mode. So much better. This game is very hard and it would be nice to score a victory and then actually be able to sit back and enjoy watching the replay. Currently, the replays are hardly worth watching.

Keep adding more new tracks. And stay with just road tracks - we love 'em.

Keep improving it and I'll keep buying it. With the improvements mentioned above, it would be an easy 5 Stars.

A month ago, I bought the PlayStation Move Mayhem Bundle. Let me say, this wasn't a real mayhem to unbox than it was to setup! To break it down, I have a mini-review/summary for each product.

PlayStation Move Wand:
The PlayStation Move Wand is a great piece of hardware. Compared to the Wiimote, it is at least 100 times more sensitive and accurate than that device. In respect to Kinect, it is ideal for the hardcore gamer who needs the precise controls for shooter titles or very active games. As well, it is snappy and feels fluid to use in games that support it. What makes it so great is the ball on top which is tracked by the PlayStation Eye to bring the best precision in the business. If only they could use a Kinect Bar to track instead...

The accessibility of the buttons is very each to reach once you get the mapping down. The two buttons [Select] and [Start], which have very little use, are a bit awkward to press but chances are you will never have to use them. Most of the time though, I found myself using the [Move] button the most along side [T]. For those who don't have the rapid reflexes needed in shooter games, it is pretty responsive and mainly relies on the input lag which is little to none in Killzone 3 and Resistance 3. Overall, a great peripheral that trumps the Wii in every aspect.

PlayStation Move Navigation:
This part is an extra joystick for those who don't want to awkwardly hold a Dualshock 3 controller when playing. The grip on the device is great but can get a bit sweaty after awhile. There isn't much that I can say other than that it is an extension of the Move set to broaden your gameplay.

PlayStation Eye:
The Eye is the backbone of the whole operation. Without it, that fancy little ball on top wouldn't do much, if anything. The Eye is like a pre-Kinect camera tracker that was used on the PlayStation Move. Standalone, it isn't very useful but for what it is used for now, it is pretty good. I wish Microsoft would pair Kinect with the Move for the ultimate experience. But, this is for another discussion at another time.

Sharpshooter Tool:
The Sharpshooter is a great peripheral for the hardcore shooter fan in your family. This is needed for Move fans playing shooter games and want the full experience. When playing Killzone 3 with it, the accuracy, precision, and control was better than without it. Lack of access of the Move Wand is compensated by being present on the Sharpshooter as well with [X] and [O] being accessible with the Move Navigation controller. The one thing I love about the Sharpshooter is the reload button at the bottom. While I would love if it was an actual piece that partially slid out or had to slid out and pushed back in to reload, it is still pretty realistic.

Killzone 3:
If you could, please read the review here at [...]. I couldn't do any better job than the guys at Gameinformer.

Resistance 3:
Again, please go to [...]. I can't really write a review for the game myself.

review_title: Good FPS if you like historic war games
review_text:
I'm a fan of the COD and MOH series WWII games and am less attracted to jungle war games. I didn't enjoy MOH:PA as much as the European theater games. I also didn't care for Men of Valor that much. This game differs from many of the Vietnam war games in that it takes place mostly in the city. While some reviewers see that as a negative, I see it as a positive. Just a personal preference. In fact, I have to credit Amazon reviews for pointing out the urban setting which is the reason I bought it.

I thought the graphics, weapon selection, and game play were good enough for the game to be enjoyable even in 2009. The game has auto-saves as well as a limited number of manual saves. The number of manual saves depends on the difficulty level. I played on HARD, so I got three. Playing on NORMAL gets ten manual saves. The difficulty level also controls how easily you get killed. The difficulty settings seem about average. I normally play on the default difficulty, but was able to play this on HARD with only a few occasions where I used all my saves sooner than I should have.

The story line was tied to historic events giving the game some educational value like the MOH and COD games. An interesting twist is that you get to play the part of a Vietcong after you complete the American campaign. I found that to be a nice bonus.

The game didn't take a long time to get through, but it is definitely worth the $15 I paid for it.

I begin by saying that I am not a devoted fighting games enthusiast, but I enjoy SF2, SSF2T:HD and SF4 the most out of all the fighting games I have ever played. I used to own all of the SF2s on the Super Famicom/SNES and had a Capcom Fighting Stick.

I bought this on around the 21st of Feb at a local retailer in Hong Kong (1/F of 188 Oriental Shopping Centre in Wan Chai) for HK$498. I understand that play-asia.com has them in stock too. The stick is primarily intended for use with SF4. I haven't watched the video review above, and have only used it for around 2 hours total. Before that I had used the DS3 for around an hour, hence why I went shopping for a stick. I haven't tried it with any other fighting games.

The Dominator was for me the cheapest and most easily available alternative to the really rather expensive Hori sticks which I could find locally. The Horis were going in the shops for around HK$1300 and even play-asia.com's cheapest Hori was just below HK$1000. So for the price of that I could have (though I didn't) bought 2 of these and gotten my mates over to play! Plus I have already spent a lot of money and space on other gaming kit, such as 2 Rock Band guitars, the drums, and a Logitech G25 mounted on a Playseat full racing seat setup...

The stick itself really does resemble that in the picture. The blue LEDs are slightly less tacky-looking in real life than they are in the picture, particularly as the translucent plastic used in the base, while acceptable, will not go particularly well with your Ligne Rosset lounge chairs. The button action is acceptable, although I find that MP is a bit firmer than the rest for some reason. They are all coated with somewhat cheap-looking chrome paint.

The stick (the ball of which is also coated with the slightly cheap-looking chrome paint) is far better than the D-pad on the DS3. Ther eis an acceptable 8-way clicky action to it. Fireball-style moves can still be a bit hard to pull off, but this probably has to do with the angle with which I am using the stick (can't put it on the table) plus the fact that I haven't used an arcade stick for SF-style games for well-over a year. It's superb for dragon punches and charging moves. I haven't played much with Zangief so I decline to attempt to grade my spinning piledriver attempts. It does make using E.Honda a real pleasure though.

I should point out that I am having trouble executing the Ken kata-throw (as mentioned in a 1up guide - MK followed quickly by throw) as well as effectively cancelling into focus moves, but I think that is also probably more a matter of timing than anything else.

I have not tried out the macro function as I would rather develope l337 sk1llz or die trying. ;)

Overall, as you may be able to tell from what I have said above, the build quality of the stick is acceptable, given the price. Furthermore, and more importantly, it is inherently usable as a fighting stick. I intend to try it with Soldner-X and 1942 Joint Strike when I have some free time, but I see no reason why it would be any worse for those if it can put up with SF4.

The only reason I have rated this stick 4 stars instead of 5 is that it's a bit cheap-looking and is obviously not made out of super-high-end components. However, in this case, and particularly given the cost of the Hori sticks, it's just a matter of getting what you pay for. Plus it's not like one is going to be able to use this stick for 10 years or more anyway (as my still-working Capcom Fighting Stick with its outdated SNES/Super Famicom connector will tell you). Highly recommended for cash-strapped fighting enthusiasts.

review_text:
OK here it goes: Vietcong 2 is a great game despite the lack of jungle fever meaning instead of fighting through the jungles of vietnam you fight through the urban jungle of Hue City in S. Vietnam battling through the Tet Ofensive of 68'.

The atmosphere in the U.S. campaign is pretty intense because you battle through the streets of Hue City and from house to house, building to building, street to street urban fighting. Graphics are right on par with this series and since I have a powerful rig, I was able to use the highest settings for the game. The detail looks better than in 2003 Vietcong but for some reason the vegitation looks the same or close to what it looked like in Vietcong.

Hopefully they will release some more coop maps here soon or release a map editor so players can design their own maps for coop and other types of multiplayer game types.

Overall, a great sequal to the Vietcong series. Most reviewers are giving this bad reviews because of it's brief campaigns and lack of replay value but don't be fooled, I've played a lot of war shooters and the Vietcong series including this one is one of the best!

review_title: RPM Racing:  A very overlooked racing game for the SNES!
review_text:
RPM Racing came out early in the SNES cycle, and was soon steamrolled by Super Mario Kart, among others. But this game had some unique features...

- The best of which, actually, was to be able to create your own track and then race your best times. I'm sure in today's racing games you can do the same and post them to the internet...so this was an idea before it's time.

- Nothing was more fun then to plant a mine right behind your friend, or mine an entire turn and watch them blow up for about 30 seconds while they ate your nitro dust

- This game got REALLY challenging near the end, and the CPU showed no mercy either.

Looking back, obviously graphically this game sucks compared not only to other SNES games but definitely to the next gen ones. The same green background isn't going to do it for most people. And only 3 vehicles to choose from probably won't either.

For most, the sequel (Rock and Roll Racing) gives you a better idea where the developers got it right and learned from RPM Racing. That game has one of the better racing soundtracks in it prior to Gran Turismo for the PS1 IMO.

But if you want to see where it all got started, or if you're dying from road rage and just want to see the joy of blowing up your opponents with some mines, this game will definitely do that, and at a real cheap price to boot.

review_title: The Good, The Bad, and The Blue
review_text:
The Good:
I was pretty excited to get a blue controller for my X Box and found that it looked pretty similar to the official one in terms of overall shape and coloration. That being said, I found it was noticeably lighter than the controller Microsoft is selling, which was not too bad since my hands cramp up fairly easily and were less tired by a lighter controller.

The joysticks were also decently grippy and resisted palm sweat… but also resisted movement because they were honestly stiffer than I expected.

The Blue Controller Question:
If you’re on the market for a blue controller, this one could be a huge pain or a huge win depending on who you are. My cousin (who hasn’t touched an x box in years) was stoked to play with a brand new bright blue controller, and didn’t really notice the stiffness of the face buttons or joysticks. But I’ll be complaining for a bit about the low sensitivity and amount of effort my thumbs need for a while.

So, in short, this could be a great controller for someone new to gaming, but most other people (myself included) will probably want to save themselves some disappointment and get the real deal.

I’m going to get right down to it because I’ve now had two complete duds in a row on the Switch. I don’t think there’s been an FPS shooter on the Switch that I haven’t enjoyed from the retro glory of Ion Fury to the brilliance of Elite Sniper 4. That is, until I played Metro Redux. I get what the developers were going for. This is a grim, post-apocalyptic survival horror. The whole world is dark and blighted with vicious mutated creatures wandering the landscape. The problem is the game fails in just about everything it tries to do.

I was playing a section where I was being led through a tunnel and it actually wasn’t that bad. It was atmospheric and intriguing. Then I got to the gameplay. What a miserable, soul sucking experience. I need to get somewhere to do something, and I have an absolutely worthless compass to guide me. There is an endless number of spawning monsters attacking me and a very limited amount of ammo. It’s dark and I’m shooting while backing away as fast as I can trying to dispatch the monsters before they kill me. Maybe I kill them and if so, I frantically try to search and find something to do before the next wave comes AND I’m dead. Start over again. And again. And again. All that’s going through my head is, “I hate this game”.

One of my main criteria for playing a game is, how hard is the game to put down. In this case, I literally might give up on this game despite having played far less than the entire game because I hate picking it up. So, what do Elite Sniper 4, Doom, Ion Fury and Crysis 2 have in common? They are all FAR superior to Metro Redux and they all have lower Metacritic scores. I recently gave WRC 9 a one start because I found the game unplayable but even in THAT game, I’m able to continue on even if I come in last place in nearly every race. In this case, I’m stuck and I’m just hating the game. I’ve played games where I’ve persevered and forged on when stuck but I just don’t want to keep playing this unpleasant, unfun and ugly game. Heck, I 100 percented New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe. I’m willing to put in the work. This game is drudgery.

The game has an 80 Metacritic score and quite a few 90+ individual scores. It has an 8.2 user rating on 76 using ratings. Those are pretty good score. I found the game a dismal, dreary mess. I probably played every level in Elite Sniper 4 five to ten times. I finished Crysis 2 multiple time. FPS might be my favorite genre of all time and I’m a survival horror fan going back to the first Resident Evil game. This game is terrible. Buy it at your own risk but my suggestion is to get any of the other games I’ve mentioned and give this one a big pass.

review_title: Amazing little keyboard, can double as a blunt force weapon.
review_text:
As someone who has only ever used full sized membrane keyboards, I can say that making the switch to a 60% mechanical was quite a change. I was a little apprehensive about moving to such a small keyboard, mostly because I didn't want to deal with the hassle of shipping this keyboard back to Amazon if I hated the layout. But after about two months of reading about mechanical keyboards I had some ideas of what features I wanted, namely:
-Tenkeyless or smaller
-Linear switches
-PBT Keycaps
-Standard key layout (makes it easier to change keycaps)
-Floating key design (easier to clean)
-Dedicate arrow keys
-Metal housing or at least a metal backplate
-Some type of backlighting
-Non-Gamer design or fonts (this was a big one for me)

I did end up finding a keyboard that matched all of my criteria, the WhiteFox, but that keyboard is not easily available nor do I find spending well over $200 on a keyboard very appealing. In the end, this keyboard had nearly everything I was looking for and at a much more manageable price. So, if I had to would I buy it again?

Absolutely!

Now before I continue, there are a few things to keep in mind with this keyboard. There is obviously no numpad and the other keys like f1-f12, PageUp, PageDown, Home, End, etc. are all placed behind a function layer, so to press f5 you have to press fn + 5 or to press PageUp you press fn + U. This might sound a little confusing but its not too bad because all these secondary functions are clearly labeled on the underside of the keys that have them. So the U key has PgUp on the underside while the I,J,K,L, keys have little Up, Down, Left, Right arrows. Now, if you are someone who uses the numpad a lot then this keyboard is probably not for you, if you need to have keys like PageUp ,End, or the arrow keys readily available then you may want to look elsewhere. But if you want an amazing little keyboard in a compact design then read on.

The first thing I noticed when pulling this keyboard out of the box was just how solid it felt. Seriously, in a pinch you could knock someone across the head and I doubt you would break anything, well at least not on the keyboard. The case is a solid piece of metal which keeps the keyboard from flexing, like at all, it also lends some nice heft as well. The switches feel amazing over membrane style switches. I find myself randomly pressing the fn or menu keys simply because I like the feel of the switches so much. Each key press feels very smooth and uniform with no keys feeling lighter or heavier than the others. The keycaps are ABS, though I would have preferred PBT keycaps like on the non-RGB Poker 3. Still its not a big deal as the keycaps do feel like good quality and they do a great job at allowing the led lighting to shine through. The RGB lighting is customizable on a per-key basis which means you can change the color of each key as well as turn on and off the lighting for individual keys. You can also cycle through various lighting modes and effects. The lack of dedicated arrow keys did take some time for me to get used to but after a week I was mostly adapted to using the fn key + I,J,K,L keys in place of actual arrow keys.

If you are a little worried about making the leap to a 60% board, I say don't be. I've found that nearly all of the keys that I most often press are right at my fingertips while the less used keys are really only an extra keypress away, and the added desk space is a nice bonus too. I'm very happy I decided to pull the trigger on the awesome keyboard and I think it will be sitting on my desk for a very long time.

I have never used a mechanical keyboard with blue switches, and I wanted to try them. I have heard all sorts of stories about them and people seem to have strong opinions both for and against depending on your use scenario.

I am frequently surprised how much I end up liking things that I didn't think I would like based on the reviews. This mechanical keyboard is one of those things.

Typing is wonderful. These keys were made to type on. The feel, the click, is just a whole new awesome experience for me. Up until this point I have only used red, silver, and brown switches because I mainly game. These blue switches may be great to type on, but they are equally great to game on! The are responsive and I had no problems gaming, they were fun to use.

Are they louder than the more linear keys? Yes, but not obnoxiously so. Maybe if your in close quarters with other people, and you type a novel everyday, someone might say something. But if you have your computer in your room and use it like most of us do, for gaming and surfing the web, and stuff like that, its absolutely no problem. From some of what I have read online I thought they would be much louder than they actually are. Honestly the sound, feel, and click are really nice and I like it.

I had no problems with this keyboard but do have two minor cons which I will get into shortly. They are not enough to take any points off my rating.

This keyboard worked well. From gaming to typing it was a pleasure to use. When it arrived one of the key caps, I think the tab key, was loose and had come off the switch during shipping. I just popped it back on and it worked fine.

The rgb is zone lighting, like another keyboard I recently reviewed. This one seems to do the zone lighting a bit better. It was quite bright, and the lighting effects you can use, while they did not change the set colors on the keyboard, still had some amazing lighting effects that were fun to play with.

Build quality seems quite durable and comparable to other mechanical keyboards I have. Key switches are hot swappable which is nice. Double Shot key caps are also nice. It comes with 4 extra switches and a switch puller.

You can use it in wired or wireless mode. I prefer wired due to mainly using the keyboard for gaming. This leads me to the two minor cons I have. The first one is that where you store the 2.4G receiver in the keyboard slot, its a little loose. If you traveled with the keyboard a lot I would worry about that receiver getting misplaced or lost if it came out of the slot its in for storage. The second minor con I have is that when I plugged in the usb c cable in the back of the keyboard, it was not very tight and I tried but could not feel it snap in like you usually can. No matter how hard I pushed the cable plug seemed slightly out of the socket. This made it easy to pull out. Now after being plugged in I had no problems and it never pulled out on its own, or when I moved the keyboard. It is just something I would worry about and would feel better if it connected more firmly. The cable is long enough to use with most desktop setups.

Overall I quite like this keyboard and was surprised the rgb zone lighting looks as good as it does, and how much I enjoyed the blue switches. If your into pc gaming and computers, it is quite a bit of fun trying the different mechanical switches out there and seeing which ones you enjoy using the most. Blue switches are louder, but its not terrible and I think they have the best feel of any of the switches I have tried.

review_title: Best WW2 Tank Sim to date
review_text: When it comes to combat simulators, WW2 tank simulations have to be the rarest of the genre. The last three I remember was i44 and Panzer Elite and Panzer Commander. These sims all came out around the same time and the genre has been pretty stagnet since then. That all changed when SFK:42 hit the market. The game is based upon armored/infantry action that took place at Kharakov in the Ukraine during 1942. The game had a rocky western release as the western publisher went bankrupt soon after release. Discus who is the games RU distributor decided to with hold further funding for the products continued development (patches) and the developer Graviteam was kind of left high and dry. Graviteam did manage to release one patch that fixed some of the major bugs in the game. Several people (and I suspect some Graviteam members working incognito) also have done mods to greatly advance this simulation. There are now mods available that enhance the in game sounds, makes the AI tanks user playable (some do not have interior cockpits but function just like the original playable tanks), add more campaigns and single missions for both sides, allows missions originally written for one tank type to be handed off to the new playable tanks for both sides. In effect a mission originally written for the Panzer MkIV (one of the original playable units) can now be handed off to a Panzer MkIII (a new playable unit). There are also the Steel Panzers mods (1.3 is latest version) that corrected some other game issues (like ammo types and shell ballistics) and added even more campaigns and single missions and more playable units. The game itself is very solid running under Vista and is very immersive. The AI is very good and will surprise you on many missions in the campaigns. The game is very scalable,GFX and DM are excellent, historically accurate, and fun. Unlike its counterpart released around the same time (T-34 vs Tiger) SF:K42 does not have MP. But for SP SFK:42 surpasses T-34 vs Tiger by a very wide margin as I do believe T-34 vs Tiger only has 8 scripted SP missions. SFK:42 also includes a mission builder so you can make your own missions. One thing to keep in mind SFK:42 is a RU developed game and a WW2 Tank simulation. And because of that mods and info are not easy to locate. I know of only one site that has all the mods and another that has a few. But if you are a interested in this time of armored conflict you wont mind doing the searching to find these gems.

Nascar Heat 2002 is the most complex racing game on Game Boy Advance. The game contains 12 race tracks including Daytona 500, Pepsi 400, Phoenix International Raceway, etc. with exceptional graphics, beautiful course details, and realistic life-like features such as day, night, rain, snow, etc. You can choose the weather and other features in Option mode, along with sound effects, number of laps, and music volume. Here are some of the other modes you can choose from:

Arcade: This is a full season mode for beginners that can build their racing skills to the maximum. Plus you can focus on certain courses that give you trouble as well as mastering turns and other obstacles.
Time Trial: This is where you are alone on the track to race for the best time possible with any of the 24 different drivers in this game. Drivers include Jeff Gordon, Tony Stewart, Dale Jarrett, and other top Winston Cup racers.
Career: This mode is where you can race on all 12 tracks and earn Winston Cup points based on your performance. Lots of points will earn you a top spot on the leaderboard but several poor performances will lead to you get booted of the circuit.
Beat the Heat: This mode offers 16 race challenges that are designed by top NASCAR drivers. Challenges include completing a race in a certain amount of time, pasting a certain amount of drivers in a lap, and making sharp turns without getting a scratch on your car.
Single Race: This mode is perfect if you don't have the time to race the whole circuit. Pick any of the 12 courses with as many laps as you desire.
Multiplayer: This games multiplayer mode is one of the best for any game. Race with as many as 4 people using only one game pack to play Single Race, or with multiple packs you can compete against your friends in either Career Mode or Beat the Heat.

review_title: This is the gun you've been looking for.
review_text:
I own a wii zapper. I have tried the Nyko Perfect Shot twice and I broke them both. That being said, the Hand Cannon is the gun to get.

The Hand Cannon is amazing! It's huge, has beautiful scroll work down the barrel, and has a nice rubberized grip. The white plastic is a perfect match to the standard wii remote, not only in color, but in durability and gloss. The handle is not too thick (I'm looking at you, Nyko!), and the trigger spring is just right. The wii remote snaps firmly in place and feels very safe and snug in this firmly secure enclosure.

The only thing I could ask from the Hand Cannon is that the handle could use more weight to fill out the balance a little better, but this is a minor issue and does not detract from my five star rating. Also keep in mind that the crosshairs will not work during game play. This is because of how the wii is set up and is not at all a defect or detraction from the awesomeness of the Hand Cannon.

I didn't not purchase from this site, but had mine imported from the UK for a better price. Waiting a month for its arrival, I would almost have rather just bought it from here. Just do it, you'll forever love yourself!

First off do not listen to the negativity. This is the highest quality Wii gun peripheral I have seen. The trigger action is smooth and pulls straight back. The clips and retentioner for the wii-mote are well designed. The rubber grip handle has a nice feel to it. This is not the usual flimsy piece of plastic optimized for 5 year olds and people with pencil wrists. My only regret was not ordering the black rubber grip version as well when it was available.

Remember with this attachment it was only released in the UK. Hence why they are currently unavailable and hard to find (Try amazon.co.uk). I write this review for any looking to purchase one of these beauties. I have two, one that I use and one that I have left sealed in the box.

The other thing to remember is that the wii-mote is placed forward in front of the grip further than the other gun attachments. What this means is it feels like it has weight to it (like you would expect from a giant over powered revolver) adding to the feel.

In summation if this controller is too much for you and you can't handle the weight go get a dumbell and do some curls then try again!

And try amazon.co.uk for this if it is not available in the US site.

review_title: Norton Internet Security removed it upon downloading it
review_text:
What the hey, there are worse ways for Cheap Me to spend a buck than to buy a cute game for my kids. They like match-3 games and we even had a cat named Cobi (g). But as soon as I downloaded the game with the Amazon Downloader, my Norton Internet Security sprung to life, identified the setup executable as containing a virus (suspicious.mystic) and quarantined it.

I realize that this was a possible false positive on the part of NIS; such things happen. But better safe than sorry, hence one star.

I also called Amazon to alert them of the possible virus. The courteous person whom I spoke with assured me of two (actually a bit contradictory) things, first that all software offered for download on the Amazon site has been thoroughly checked for viruses and second that she would send a request that this item be further tested. She also refunded my buck, no prompting required.

So it was eventually a benign customer experience, luckily one that my kids didn't witness, meaning no lower-lip disappointment ensued. If it turns out that after further testing Amazon confirms that this was a false positive, I hope that they will post that fact in a comment, since my reason for this review was not to hinder anyone's potential income stream.
